Hesolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
1. That for the 1949 and subsequent taxation years, the provision under which the 10 per cent tax rate on the first $10,000 of income of a corporation applies only to one of several related companies be amended so that the test of relationship of companies shall be ownership of 70 per cent or more of all the issued common shares of capital stock of the corporation instead of mere control.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I begin the discussion of the Income Tax Act resolutions, there are one or two matters connected with excise tax to which I should like to refer. I believe this would be the appropriate time to do so.
The hon. member for Melfort asked an interesting question as to the status of American contracting firms bidding on Canadian projects, having success in their bids and then bringing their equipment across the line to work on such projects. Obviously if they were able to bring equipment across without duty and sales tax they would be in a preferred position in comparison with Canadian contractors. I referred this matter to the deputy minister of national revenue in charge of customs and excise, and perhaps, for the information of all hon. members, I might be permitted to put his opinion on the record.
Under the customs tariff the contractors' equipment mentioned would be subject to payment of customs duty and sales tax in the ordinary course, but where materials are owned by a United States concern who have been given a contract by Canadian interests to perform certain operations in this country and who require the use of equipment which is of a special nature and not available here, it is the practice of the department to submit the facts to the governor general in council with a view to obtaining authority for collection of the duty and sales tax on a proportionate basis, conditional on exportation of the equipment within a specified length of time. It is only where inquiries made by .the department have established the fact that no Canadian interests would be prejudiced that such submissions are forwarded to council.
I should like to make a short statement with regard to the first income tax resolution to be found in the ways and means resolutions now before us. While I am piloting these resolutions through the committee, the Minister of Finance of course will actually put the bill through. I am not a lawyer, and income tax legislation is without doubt the most technical of all the legislation on our statute books. Nevertheless most hon. members are
Income Tax Act
not lawyers, so it may be an advantage so far as the resolution stage is concerned to have the general intent of these resolutions explained in layman's language, and that is what I intend to do.
The Minister of Finance has told me that between the first reading and the second reading of the bill at least one week will be allowed to elapse, during which time hon. members who are interested in this type of legislation can study the bill. He has asked me to repeat the invitation he has given to all members of the house to avail themselves of the services and help and advice of the many excellent and competent officials in the Department of Finance and of National Revenue who have worked on this legislation.
The first of the Income Tax Act resolutions relates to the ten per cent tax concession which was made last year to small business. You will remember that before last year we had a flat thirty per cent tax on the profits of corporations, and it was felt that that bore down too heavily on the small businessman. So for the first time in the history of our tax legislation we introduced a graduated scale of corporation taxation somewhat similar to' the graduated scale we have always had in: connection with personal income tax.
The rates were changed to ten per cent on the first $10,000, and then, to ensure that there was no revenue loss, the rate was raised to thirty-three per cent on the profits beyond that figure. That actually meant that a company with profits less than $77,000 a year would gain under this legislation, while a company with profits over that would have to pay heavier taxes.
The intent of the legislation was not necessarily to help small business; the intent was to help the small businessman. There are many wealthy men in this country who have a great number of small businesses and who derive from those businesses large incomes of perhaps $50,000 to $100,000 per year. If this ten per cent rate were applied to all small businesses which had profits of less than $10,000 a year, it would be possible for such a man to have an income of from $50,000 to-$100,000 a year and pay only this ten per cent corporation tax rate, whereas another man with the same income, but derived solely from one company, would be paying ten per cent on the first $10,000 and thirty-three per cent on the income above that.
If the ten per cent rate was to be applied1 to every company then it would be possible for certain types of businesses to break up into individual units. For example, chain

Income Tax Act
stores could be broken up so that every store was a separate corporation which would pay the ten per cent rate. The result would be that the aggregate corporation income would be subject only to the ten per cent rate. On the other hand, there are many industries which could not be broken up in that fashion. In my own riding there are mines and pulp and paper mills where the final sales are at the end of their production, the sale of ore or concentrates or paper.
Last year we tried to devise legislation which would help the people we wanted to help, the small businessmen who were struggling to expand their businesses, by relieving them of this heavy thirty per cent tax and substituting the ten per cent rate. However, to protect against abuses such as I have mentioned we limited that to one of a number of controlled companies. The majority shareholders of those controlled companies will be the ones who will designate which of the companies shall receive this concession of ten per cent tax on the first $10,000.
When the minister was piloting the bill through the house, hon. members on both government and opposition sides pointed out some of the factors which were involved, and suggested that it might prove to be a hardship on the minority shareholders in controlled companies. At that time the minister gave the house assurance that if during the year experience showed that this was inflicting hardship on the type of businessman we intended to help, changes would be made, and made retroactive to cover the 1949 tax year. When I appeared before the Senate I gave the same assurance.
During this past year it has been found that the present legislation, while of good intent, has hurt one class of businessman in Canada. It often happens that someone, perhaps a returned veteran, wants to start a small business in a small town, possibly a garage. He cannot raise the money in the ordinary way, so he turns to what you might call the local capitalist, the man who has made his money in the town. This man not only has money; he has credit standing and managerial experience. I am sure that every hon. member who has small towns in his riding knows that that situation exists. Such a man may help any number of little industries to get going. He will retain control of the company during a certain period and exercise managerial control. Because of that the business is able to obtain bank and other credit.
Under the present legislation only one of such a group of small companies which had been helped by one or two local men of

money would be able to obtain this concession. Whichever company was picked out would get the concession, but the others, the minority shareholders in the other groups, would not only be denied the ten per cent concession; they would be paying a corporation tax, not at the old thirty per cent rate but at the new level of thirty-three per cent. It is for that reason that we have introduced this new resolution to expand the idea of control, not to bare control, but, as is stated in the resolution, to ownership of not more than seventy per cent of the common shares.
It is hoped by this means to expand this concession to most of the genuine small businesses in the country. At the same time the seventy per cent stipulation does not make this concession available to some of the large corporations whose business is of such an order that they could break it up into units and so avoid the normal corporation tax.
Will this be retroactive?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the assurance given by the minister, that it will cover the 1949 tax year. That was promised by the minister in the resolution speech he made last fall.

On the face of it I think this resolution is likely to commend itself to hon. members. The parliamentary assistant, however, might expand the information given in some respects. In the first place, may I ask whether, under the terms of the proposed bill, this will remain the only definition of related corporations? In the second place, is the parliamentary assistant in a position to inform the house how many corporations have been affected by the provision introduced last year in the amendment to section 36 of the act? How many small companies were benefited by the reduction in rate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
So far as the latter part of the question is concerned, of course the tax returns are not in yet. Our only knowledge comes from the correspondence we have received. Gererally the concession was greatly welcomed, but the one complaint was from this group of companies. Perhaps I should also mention that it was not in the House of Commons but rather before a Senate committee that the question was raised by various senators. I know at times the Senate is harshly dealt with in this house, but my experience in the last few years in the position I occupy has been that the Senate committees on banking and commerce and finance are of tremendous aid to our parliamentary processes. It was there that various senators put their fingers on the point that our bare control measure would inflict hardship on the very class of small businessmen in small towns whom we were seeking to aid. The

actual definition of related companies will be spelled out most carefully in the bill which will be available once the resolution passes.
That is not quite an answer to my question. I asked if this test, as proposed in the resolution, will now become the only and exclusive test to determine whether or not corporations are related.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh, no; this particular test has been applied only with relation to this special tax concession.
Again may I say that I do not think the parliamentary assistant has understood my point. Is this going to be the only test under section 36 of the act whether corporations are or are not related?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes; that is right.

Will the parliamentary assistant say what restrictions or safeguards there are to protect the department against companies subdividing into other companies, and bringing the subdivided companies within the position contemplated by the act last year and the change now being made? As I understand it, when the Minister of Finance introduced the budget he said these changes were made for the purpose of encouraging small business, and that is a most commendable purpose. The parliamentary assistant has mentioned that there are numbers of businessmen who control a number of small companies. What is there to prevent any company in Canada today from coming within the shareholder provision of this section by subdividing into units? What is there to prevent a businessman with half a dozen small companies from continuing to operate those companies, thereby escaping the heavier rate of taxation? What is there to prevent larger businesses with the same type and percentage of control from breaking up and thereby ensuring an evasion of income tax?
Let me carry it one step further. What is there to prevent a chain store, taking the example given by the parliamentary assistant, from coming into this country, opening a dozen units, and, within the control limits provided under this resolution, establishing each one of those chain stores as separate incorporations? Has anything like that been done in the last year? Are any safeguards contemplated in the bill to be introduced to implement the resolution which will prevent such a situation from arising?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not explain sufficiently why we picked on seventy per cent. If it had been ninety or ninety-five per cent, then it would have been comparatively easy to do the sort of thing the
Income Tax Act
hon. member for Lake Centre has suggested. With seventy per cent control, however, it is not merely seventy per cent control by one person but by one person or persons not dealing at arm's length. If in two or three of these companies one saw the same shareholder in the other thirty per cent of common stock, then the Department of National Revenue would say that these people are obviously not dealing at arm's length.
That is not a very strong safeguard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am assured that from the legal standpoint-and I know that is what my hon. friend is interested in-adequate safeguards have been worked out.
What are they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is why I said so clearly that while I think I am competent to explain the matter in layman's language to a layman,
I should not presume to try to explain a legal point to the hon. member for Lake Centre. I am quite sure the minister will do so when the bill is introduced. After all, resolutions are only expressions of general intent and not details of legislation.
There will be safeguards?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There will be safeguards.

Before the resolution carries there is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant. In the resolution it is stated that it is expedient to amend the Income Tax Act to provide certain things. I should like to mention a particular case having to do with income tax. If a married woman has an income in excess of $250 and under $1,000, the income of $250 is automatically deducted from her husband's exemption as a married man. That is to say, if the wife's income is $750 the husband has $500 taken off his $2,000 exemption as a married man. On the other hand, a widower keeping house, with a daughter living at home, has an exemption of $2,000 as a householder. His daughter can have an income up to $500 and it is not deducted from the widower's exemption of $2,000. This appears to be discrimination in the widower's favour to the extent of $250 compared to the situation of a married man. A married woman's income should be exempt up to $500 before any deduction is made from her husband's exemption. I believe this matter was brought up last year. Then there is the case of the married woman over sixty-five.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. member is out of order. We are discussing

Income Tax Act
amendments to the Income Tax Act, not the principles of the act. We are discussing the principles of the amendments.

The resolution reads: "Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income Tax Act", I am suggesting amendments, and therefore I do not see how you can rule me out of order. I only have one more item. A married woman over sixty-five can have an income up to $1,500 before being taxable, but in this case any income over $250 has to be deducted from her husband's exemption as a married man. If her income is in excess of $1,000, in spite of the fact that she has an exemption of $1,500, her husband loses all his status as a married man and is therefore taxed as a single man. This certainly is an unfairness in the act that should be corrected. If an additional exemption of $500 is allowed on attaining the age of sixty-five, I believe that $500 should be reflected in an adjustment of the husband's income. The wife who is over sixty-five should have an exemption of $500 in connection with her income before the surplus income affects her husband's exemption, which would make $1,000 in all after the wife attained the age of sixty-five. This situation affects many people, and as a matter of equity it should be rectified. I hope the department will see it in that way; and any change should be made retroactive to 1949.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As you pointed out, Mr. Chairman, this first resolution has to do with corporation tax. In the second place, my job here is to explain the general intent of the amendments. The points the hon. member has raised undoubtedly would be pertinent on section 9, which has to do with income tax. In fairness to myself, the hon. member read these details-as he had to, when dealing with such figures-from a manuscript, and obviously he would not expect me to remember all the facts and figures he mentioned. When the bill is before the house, however; when we are dealing with the sections concerning personal income tax, and after the minister has had the opportunity to read the remarks of my hon. friend in Hansard, I am quite sure an answer will be forthcoming.

I want to ask the parliamentary assistant for some explanation with respect to the diminishing balance of straight-line depreciation concerning income tax, and perhaps he would tell me when such questions would be appropriate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I can certainly tell the hon. member that the best time to ask the questions will be after he has had the bill in his hands and has seen the actual legal provisions contained therein. I am quite sure
[The Chairman.]
the minister will be only too anxious to explain anything that may be asked, now that we have had some little experience with that matter.
Thank you very much; I merely wanted to find out when I should ask the questions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to mention just one point in connection with the explanations that have been given. As the parliamentary assistant has stated, he does not suggest that he has the legal training to give a strictly legal interpretation of some of these matters. He then goes on to say that he is not in a position to explain some of these details, but that if this resolution is passed now, when piloting the bill through the house later on the minister will be able to give the explanations that are required.
It may well be that the items now before the committee will be adopted without variation, but the motion before the committee is that it is expedient that certain things be done. I submit that we are not in a position to say whether or not it is expedient unless at this point there is some explanation as to why these things should be done. In fact if there is any time when the explanations should be given it is at this point, because this is the time the committee states in principle whether or not certain things should be done. Then the bill carries out the stated view of the committee in clear legal phraseology. For that reason, without raising any meaningless objection, I suggest that this is the time when every explanation that is requested should be given, so that before the committee decides whether or not something is expedient, hon. members may know about it. Then it will be possible for the legal draftsman to interpret that decision in legal phraseology.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The points raised by the leader of the opposition are the very points I tried to make in my explanation. This resolution actually states that it is expedient to extend our ten per cent corporation tax rate from bare control to seventy per cent control. I suggest that the argument by hon. members today should be directed to whether or not it is expedient that we should stick to bare control or whether we should extend it to seventy per cent, eighty per cent or ninety per cent control. I certainly suggest that at the resolution stage it is not proper for me, for example, to launch into a discussion of marriage exemptions in connection with personal income tax, or the application of the diminishing balance of depreciation. The intent of this resolution is to change the announced rate of last year of ten per cent

on the first $10,000 and we must decide whether that shall apply to only one company which is barely controlled, or shall be extended to companies controlled to the extent of seventy per cent or more of the common shares.
That, I submit, is the intent of the resolution. I have tried to explain it in the only way I can, in layman's language, for the benefit of the laymen in the house, who are just as much interested in tax questions as the lawyers are. Certainly I would be the first to admit that I am not qualified, particularly at the resolution stage, to discuss the legal procedure by means of which this intent will be translated into effective legislative action. At various times there has been talk in this house about cutting down on our parliamentary procedure. One of the suggestions has been that we should get away from this resolution stage on money bills. Some are for it; some are against it. I see that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is just itching to rise to his feet-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just to keep the record straight, I think what the hon. gentleman is saying is confirmed in part by a report that was laid on the table at one time; but that recommendation was to do away with that stage of the debate when the Speaker was in the chair, not with this stage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I quite agree; but on money bills we give this extra warning, if I may call it that. It' is not just the warning given by the first reading of a normal bill; it is an extra warning, both with the Speaker in the chair and when we are in committee. Hon. members will recall that when the Speaker was in the chair nothing was said about this particular item. At that time the debate on the motion that we go into committee of ways and means covered quite a wide range, but no one mentioned the actual budget resolutions. Even here in committee, when I think we should stick to the intent of the various resolutions, there was a feeling-it may not have been the feeling of the majority-that this was another parliamentary procedure that perhaps was not as essential today as it was in the days gone by.
In any case, I have tried to explain the intent of this resolution, which is to extend this ten per cent corporation tax concession from just bare control to seventy per cent control. I have stated that as soon as these resolutions are passed the bill will be brought down, and there will be at least a week, between that time and the time the minister proceeds with it, during which the actual details may be examined.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I should speak first on this resolution, because it has perhaps been

Income Tax Act
most misunderstood in the press of the country. There seems to be a suggestion that this is a punitive section, and that it is the intention of the government to tax capital gains. On behalf of the minister I can assure you the government has no intention of trying to tax what are now understood to be capital gains. Mind you, if one pursues in academic discussion what a capital gain is, then the grocer who buys a can of vegetables for eight cents and sells it for twelve cents has made a capital gain. We say, however, that that is his way of doing business. The man who is a speculator in real estate, and who buys a property and sells it at a higher price, has also made a capital gain, but he derives his income in that manner. On the other hand, a man who makes a long-term investment and later realizes on it to his advantage is making the sort of increase in capital which, in. the case of the grocer and the real estate man, is regarded as income. These things cannot be spelled out in the law, but have to be judged on the facts of each case.
There has been some suggestion that this resolution has to do with capital gains, -but the actual effect of it is the very opposite. Far from being a punitive section, it is a beneficial section, with special effect on private companies. It may have some small application to public corporations, but because of the special financing problems of private companies, which in our present act are spelled out as being companies of seventy-five shareholders or less, it is more applicable to them. These companies have financial problems which public corporations have not got.
There are many men in this house who are in business in a small or large way who know, first of all, how hungry an expanding business is for money. There is no end. to the money which has to be poured into a business if it is to expand. Public corporations, of course, because of their good credit, can float bonds and stocks, and have these methods of financing open to them. A private company is practically limited to the plowing back of profits into the company. This practice has been followed across the country as long as we have had private companies in Canada. The second reason why these companies have had to put back into the company an unduly large percentage of their profits rather than pay them as dividends has been the attempt to make the sale of their stock, when necessary, as attractive as possible. In some years they make money and can pay dividends out of profits. In other years they do not make money, but they have to put aside a fair proportion of their profits in the good years in order to maintain a steady

dividend. All of you know what difficulty there is in attempting to realize on the forced sale of private company stock.
For these reasons these private companies, much more so than public companies, have had to pile up a considerable portion of their profits as undistributed income. If the principal shareholder should die, this problem becomes acute, because succession duties are levied and the estate must raise the cash to pay them, so the company has to be wound up. Under our present tax laws the entire volume of the undistributed profits must be assessed as income of that year. The company may have been twenty years accumulating that surplus, and yet the shareholders, because of reasons beyond their control, the most obvious one being the death of the principal shareholder, are forced, if the company has to be wound up, to pay income tax in one year at our present rates on that entire amount.
This problem is not new. It was with us during the war, and in 1939 the Ives commission was set up to ascertain in what way, fair to both the crown-that is, the people of Canada who expect to get a fair tax return out of these companies-and to the private companies who in good faith established these surpluses, this problem could be settled. The Ives commission made recommendations which were carried out. They provided, first of all, for a graduated scale of income tax to be paid on this surplus. It is detailed in the Income War Tax Act, section 94. Section 96 of the act gives the sliding rate which varies between fifteen per cent and thirty three per cent, depending not on the total income of the shareholder but on the actual dividend which he got from the company. Of course that is not quite the fairest way, because the actual shares he had in the company might not reflect his total income. A very rich man may have a small share in the company, and he would get by with a low rate. Another man may have his total investment in that company, and because of the graduated scale applied to the actual dividend payable, he may pay quite heavily.
The second thing which was noticed in consideration of the Ives commission report was that many of these payments were tax-free payments, such as payments to other corporations and payments to persons who are non-taxable such as including trustees of pension funds. We thought-at this time it would be proper, eleven years after the Ives commission investigation, to bring forward another optional proposal for companies that want to avail themselves of it. There is nothing forced in this. Any private company that wants to do these things can relieve itself of this problem which will occur if it

has a winding up. The resolution says that the company may elect to pay fifteen per cent on undistributed income held by the corporation at the end of the 1949 tax year, or it may if it wishes, pay a tax of fifteen per cent on undistributed income earned thereafter equal to the dividends distributed from time to time by the corporation during the period when the undistributed income was earned. In other words, it is a matching provision. Some companies may not care to avail themselves of this provision, but others will. At least we are now opening up an avenue whereby these private companies, with these special financial problems which public companies do not have, can put themselves in shape, if they so wish, to meet the problem which will occur if there should be a forced winding up of the company.

On this resolution a question naturally arises as to its scope. The resolution specifies "private companies". It reads as follows:
That in order to permit a private company to pay tax on undistributed income so that it may capitalize the undistributed income, the company may elect-
[DOT]-to do certain things. In dealing with this subject in a statement to the house at pages 1217 and 1218 of Hansard on March 28, the Minister of Finance did not make reference to private companies. The expression that he used, referring apparently to the same subject, was "closely-held corporations". There can be closely-held corporations that are not private in nature. Depending on the definition of "closely-held" there might be some private corporations that might not come within the definition of close holdings of stock. I think there should be some clarification of the scope of this resolution. In his statement the parliamentary assistant dealt only with private companies. The resolution mentions only private companies. We wish to know precisely what companies are included.
I was interested to note that the parliamentary assistant dealt with this question of freeing surpluses. There is some ground, of course, for what he said about the relative problem of private companies, on the one hand, and companies that are not private, on the other, as to their sources of further capital. However, when the hon. gentleman refers to certain disquiet in the mind of the public in relation to the intent of this resolution, may I say to him that that disquiet has its foundation in things that have emanated from the Department of National Revenue and from the government.
In the past the impression has gone abroad, and there is foundation for it, whether it was the intention of the government to
Income Tax Act
create that impression or not, that the government proposed to wield the big stick and to compel corporations to distribute surpluses. For example, I refer to a Canadian Press dispatch of January 11, which appeared in most Canadian newspapers, and which reads as follows:
The revenue department has stepped up its campaign to free large surpluses of unused and undistributed income accumulating in corporation treasuries, a government spokesman said today.
There is that mysterious individual, "the government spokesman," who crops up periodically. I continue:
Corporations have been asked to use the surpluses for expansion and development or pay them to shareholders or face additional tax action by the government.
The government move is designed to help keep the economy buoyant by stimulating the flow of surpluses held by corporations for a period of years, the spokesman said.
Corporations showing a reluctance to free the surpluses are being told by registered letter that the department considers the undistributed income as being actually distributed to the shareholders as dividends, and that the shareholders will be taxed as having received this additional income.
This power is vested in the department under federal income tax laws. The spokesman said the corporations, for the most part, are co-operating with the department and the threat likely will not materialize in many cases.
The spokesman said a shareholder certainly would complain to the corporation executive if he were being taxed on money which he did not receive. The corporation thus would be forced either to pay the shareholder the amount of tax charged by the government or else actually distribute its surpluses as dividends.
Corporations which feel they have good reasons for retaining the surpluses are given a chance by the department to state their case, the spokesman said.
In some instances, corporations had put aside money for future building purposes or for purchase of additional property, or for other business reasons.
If they can show that the amount put aside is reasonable and is being put to use as quickly as possible, then the department would give them every consideration.
I have intimated, sir, that whether or not the government intended to create the impression, statements of that kind, and actions of the kind referred to in this government release under the name of threats, have created a feeling of disquiet throughout the country.
Where money is required, certainly it is within the function of this parliament and it is the duty of this parliament to enact laws to impose the burden of taxation, and impose it equitably. It is another thing, Mr. Chairman, to put in the hands of the executive branch of government a power which permits them to say: We are going to pass individual judgment on the way your executive or your board of directors does its business; we are going to say that in our opinion you are carrying an unduly large

Income Tax Act
surplus, and because we entertain that opinion, we are going to require you to distribute that surplus. In the next case the government may look at another business corporation and say: Well, we will not take as stiff a view of your case; we are not going to interfere with you. There is a very great danger in a situation of that kind, where power is vested in the executive branch of government to discriminate between various taxpayers. It is a most serious matter; and when you find that power, which is capable of very discriminatory use, vested in those who talk in terms of threats, it is a matter of which parliament should take note.
I say, sir, that if the parliamentary assistant is right in saying that there is a feeling of disquiet throughout the country in relation to this resolution, it is not, I believe, so much because of the bare terms of the resolution as it is because of the history of what has preceded it. I wish to say simply this in regard to corporation surpluses. If a time comes when there is a severe business recession, we shall be very glad to see corporations that are large employers of labour in this country possessing some surpluses with which to carry on. Where corporations have been denuded of the surpluses which, with prudent management, they have put aside for a rainy day, and they find themselves in a depression or recession of business without adequate surpluses to draw on to finance operations, we cannot expect them to be able to carry on and maintain employment and their business as they would be able to do if they had those reserves to draw on which prudent management dictates should be available for times of reduced business.
There are corporations in this country today, particularly those that are interested in the export of certain commodities, where export markets have been closed to them, that are already very glad to have some reserves to fall back on. What I am saying in general is this: that it is the function of management, broadly speaking, in relation to the needs of a business, in relation to the desire to maintain continued stable employment and the position of the company in the community and the country, to build its stability on the creation of surpluses in good . times. All wise corporations are doing it today; and it is the duty of management, in good times, to create that umbrella for a rainy day. I hope, sir, that this government is not going to inject itself, by arbitrary exercise of powers that are open to very discriminatory use, into those situations and say to company A: You distribute $100,000; to company B: We will take a different view of your case; you will distribute $20,000; to
	.
company C: We will not ask you to distribute anything. That situation, sir, is fraught with great danger of abuse, and I do urge that a statement should be made on the part of the government reassuring those who are concerned in this matter in all parts of the country that there is to be no wielding of the big stick; that the administration of the taxation statutes of this country is going to be fair and equitable, and that no attempt is going to be made to use powers that are capable of discrimination in this fashion.
I now turn to one other subject which the parliamentary assistant raised in his introductory statement on this resolution. He said it is not the policy of the government to tax capital gains. Then he went on, as I understood him, to suggest that in some respects the tax on income today can be regarded as, in fact, a tax on capital gains.
I should like to say a word or two on that subject. Again a feeling of. grave disquiet has been created throughout the country on this subject of the taxation of capital gains, and this feeling stems directly from an authoritative interpretation placed upon the Income War Tax Act by the courts of this country. In his budget speech, as reported at page 1217, the Minister of Finance said:
During the past year there has been considerable uncertainty in the mining industry with regard to the position of prospectors and those who are engaged in developing our mineral resources. From the early forties onward, it has been the practice to interpret the law as not subjecting to tax gains made by bona fide prospectors and developers in discovering and proving up mining properties. As the house knows, our Income Tax Act was completely rewritten, and the new act has been in force since the beginning of 1949. The new act contains no clear-cut authority for the practice which has been followed during the past decade. The position under the law of these important groups should be clarified, and we are proposing this year to introduce an amendment which should allay the fears of many who have in recent months been concerned about this matter.
I believe the reference there is probably to-resolution No. 3. Then the minister continued:
Perhaps I might also take this opportunity, in view of recent public interest in the question, to assure the house that it is not the policy of the-government to tax capital gains. Under any income tax law there is always a very difficult problem in drawing a line between gains which are profits-from carrying on a trade or business and those which are not. To my knowledge no tax legislation has ever been passed in any country that has removed all doubts on this score. In England, where our basis of income tax had its origin, the matter has been settled almost entirely by the courts,
. taking into account the facts in each individual case.
Then the minister adds these significant words:
Much as I would like to introduce greater certainty, I do not believe that it can be done satisfactorily by legislation.

Then he proceeds, in effect, to put forward his panacea for this problem of disquiet in the public mind by saying that provision is being made for the more expeditious hearing of cases before the income tax appeal board, and permitting taxpayers in such cases to go directly to the exchequer court, if they so desire.
It will take more than the statement of the minister on that occasion or that of the parliamentary assistant today to allay the very grave fears and disquiet created in the mind of the public by recent authoritative decisions as to the meaning of certain expressions in the Income Tax Act. It comes down to this, that what have been regarded by the public as capital gains have been interpreted in a strict sense by the courts as not constituting capital gains but being, in effect, income. Therefore they have been made subject to tax.
In a technical sense the Minister of Finance may be quite right in saying that it is not government policy to tax capital gains. He might be quite right in a technical sense if he were to say, as the Minister of National Revenue said to me about a month ago in reply to a question I asked him when the orders of the day were called, that the government is not taxing capital gains- because the Minister of National Revenue did make that statement in the house. While it may be right in a technical sense, it is not right in the sense in which that expression has come to be understood by the public. That, it seems to me, is the feature of the situation which cannot be overlooked or sidestepped by the government.
The fact of the matter is that gains which have been regarded by people in the mining industry, those engaged in the development of that industry, and also by people in business generally, as being gains in the nature of capital, have now come as a result of certain decisions-one in particular-to be regarded as income by judicial interpretation of the Income War Tax Act.
I wonder if the hon. member would give the facts of the case to which he has referred?

Yes, I intend to refer to that case, and I would hope that my hon. friend, whose constituency is interested in the development of mining, would have something to say about the case. The decision to which I am about to refer is one which has struck a serious blow, according to my understanding of the situation, at the development of the mining industry in Ontario and in other parts of Canada.

speechtext: All right.

The case to which I referred is the recent decision in the Exchequer Court of Canada in the case of W. J. McDonough v. the Minister of National Revenue. That was a decision by Mr. Justice Cameron and I think it is one which any hon. member would wish to treat with high respect. At the same time I submit that having regard to the very unfortunate effect that this decision has had on investment in-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Once again I am informed- I am speaking as a layman-that this case has been appealed to the supreme court, so when my hon. friend says that the decision is most unfortunate I submit that he is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the case is being appealed to the supreme court it would be sub judice.

The parliamentary assistant began this afternoon by disclaiming any knowledge of the legal aspects of these resolutions or any intention of discussing them from that point of view. I am not proposing to discuss whether this decision was right or wrong; I accept the decision as it stands. I am simply dealing with the effect of the decision on the mind of the public. I am not undertaking to say whether the decision is right or wrong. I just finished saying that I treat the decision of Mr. Justice Cameron in the exchequer court with the utmost respect.
The department is acting as though it were correct.

It is not my province in this house to quarrel with that decision, to argue whether it is or is not correct. It is not from that point of view that I approach the decision. The basis on which I do approach it is the qualifying words in the passage I read from the speech made by the Minister of Finance in this house on March 28 when he said this:
Much as I would like to introduce greater certainty, I do not believe that it can be done satisfactorily by legislation.

We who are sitting here as a parliament must take account of situations that are created as a result of decisions delivered in the courts. Having regard to the situation created by this decision we must ask ourselves whether that decision ought or ought not to be redressed in this parliament by legislation. My argument is that it ought to be redressed by legislation. Wherever there is a situation at all comparable with that which was before the court in the McDonough case then I submit that parliament must take cognizance of it and by legislation remove the grounds that have given rise to a feeling in the mind of the public that we have entered a period where capital gains are being taxed, a reversal of the understanding in the past of the business and mining communities as to the basis of taxation of gains. [DOT]
I think it is quite clear that what I have to say does not trespass in any respect on the rule followed in the house in connection with the correctness or incorrectness of matters before the courts or under appeal. In this case the taxpayer who was appealing had received some stock in a company in consideration of having conveyed to that company an interest in certain mining properties. When he came to realize on part of his stock the government stepped in and proposed to tax him upon it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Which part of the stock? That is the key of the whole thing.
If my hon. friend wants me to go into this in great detail I shall be happy to do so. Up until this moment he has been trying to confine me in my approach to this question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend referred to the decision as being an unfortunate decision. I may not be well versed in the law but I should think that when there is an appeal to the supreme court the fact that a member of parliament of the high standing of my hon. friend has referred publicly in a place where he is privileged to the decision as being an unfortunate decision could not help but affect the standing of the case before the court. Then when he comes to the actual case he does not go into it thoroughly. There were two blocks of stock, the stock the taxpayer actually got for his claim and the stock on which he had an option.
Is the parliamentary assistant trying to make my speech?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

The parliamentary assistant attempts to stop me at one point from discussing the case and then in the next breath says that I should go into it further.

speechtext: I do not think it is in order to discuss a case that is under appeal to the supreme court because it would be sub judice. It is difficult for the hon. member to discuss that case without affecting the judgment and I think it would be much better not to discuss it.

I respect fully what you have said and your feelings in relation to it, but notwithstanding the difficulty which the parliamentary assistant has sought to create I wish to make perfectly clear what I am proposing to do. I shall be quite glad to go into the facts of the case in great detail, or to refrain from doing so, according to your direction. What I wish to put before the committee is an interpretation of the law and I can do that without further reference to the facts of the case. I urge upon the committee that the situation is such that it calls for an amendment of the act. That leaves me in the position in which I started. I am not attempting to quarrel with the decision, to argue that it is right or wrong. When I spoke of its unfortunate effect I was referring to the feeling of disquiet and fear that it has created in the mind of the public. Referring to certain authorities, the court said this:
But the mere fact that a transaction is an Isolated one does not exclude it from the category of trading or business transactions of such a nature as to attract income tax to the profit therefrom.
I pass over any reference to the application of that rule to the facts before the court in view of what you have said. Reference is made in this judgment to a statement of the law in another case of which I think parliament ought to take note. It is this:
It is quite a well-settled principle in dealing with questions of assessment of income tax, that where the owner of an ordinary investment chooses to realize it, and obtains a greater price for it than he originally acquired it at, the enhanced price is not profit in the sense of schedule D of the Income Tax Act of 1942 assessable to income tax. But it is equally well established that enhanced values obtained from realization or conversion of securities may be so assessable, where what is done is not merely a realization or change of investment, but an act done in what is truly the carrying on, or carrying out, of a business. The simplest case is that of a person or association of persons buying and selling lands or securities speculatively, in order to make gain, dealing in such investments as a business, and thereby seeking to make profits. There are many companies which in their very inception are formed for such a purpose, and in these cases it is not doubtful that, where they make a gain by a realization, the gain they make is liable to be assessed for income tax.
I say with some degree of confidence that it has been the understanding of the business
Income Tax Act
and mining communities that gains made on individual transactions in the development of mining properties or the realization of assets, gains from such transactions which are not carried on by traders or people whose business it is to engage in that kind of transaction, were not considered as income gains but as capital gains and therefore not taxable. I contend that the alarm created in the public mind is so serious that its remedy cannot be confined to the limited type of legislation envisaged in the third resolution. I submit that what is required is broader legislation in order to make it quite clear that the investing public, the public engaged in the development of resources, may be able to depend upon a continued application of the law according to the understanding that has prevailed for a good many years. In view of the fact that a decision has been made in the exchequer court to the contrary, that will now require legislation. As I understand it the third resolution offers some legislation, but it does not cover the whole field.
The subject of taxation of capital gains is one that can have the most widespread and unfortunate results, not simply if capital gains are in fact being taxed but even if there is in the mind of the public an apprehension that capital gains are or are about to be taxed. Therefore I urge that this subject be approached broadly in view of the way in which it has arisen and the fear in the mind of the public, and that we have ample legislation now to remove all fear and apprehension as to the result.

I rise to ask a question. I should like to say first that when the hon. member for Eglinton started to speak I thought I could agree with him almost completely. After his talk for forty-five minutes or thereabouts and going around the matter so much I am so mixed up I do not know whether I can or whether I cannot. When he said that people are concerned about undistributed profits, capital gains, or whatever you want to call them, he certainly hit the mark because it is a matter about which there is considerable concern throughout the country. I have read the resolution as many times as I think necessary and I am still not clear about it. It is still ambiguous even after the explanation of the parliamentary assistant. The clause seems to me to be important, not for what is offered but rather for what it threatens to do in the future. I still cannot see what a private businessman would gain by taking advantage of the provision unless at some time in the future the government is going to tax his undistributed income. The parliamentary assistant stated this afternoon

it would allow a businessman to plow back profits. I cannot see that at all. He might as well keep his profits in surplus as have them tied up in capital. What advantage is there? Therefore I say again that I wish the parliamentary assistant would tell the businessmen of Canada in a nutshell how on earth they benefit from this clause. I cannot understand it.
