Quite right. It gets down to the other expression, "closely held".
(Mr. Thatcher.]
It would have been better to use that expression because the expression "private company" suggests something quite different.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Turning to the next point, I want to speak with as much heat as he did when he read an unmentioned press clipping.
I said it was a Canadian Press dispatch. It appeared in a number of papers, and I gave the date of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
He quoted this government
spokesman. When the government wants a spokesman the spokesman is identified by name. If there is going to be an announcement of policy the Minister of Finance or someone authorized by him will make it. I know the hon. member does not want to distort things. Having started off by describing it as a press release by an unmentioned government spokesman he then called it a government release. It was not a government release. Government announcements of policy will come from the Minister of Finance.
Turning to the hon. member for Moose Jaw, I will try to explain the matter by saying that if you want to be academic then the purchase of some small article by a grocer for 30 cents today and the sale tomorrow for 40 cents is a capital gain. On the other extreme is the example of a member of parliament who comes here at the beginning of a session and buys a house for $15,000. Four years later, because of reasons which the electorate think sufficient, he may have to dispose of his house and he sells it for $20,000. That is the other extreme of a capital gain. Without any doubt that capital gain is not taxable, but the actual income which comes from the daily or weekly buying and selling of goods and chattels, which is the business of the man, is certainly not a capital gain as the people of Canada understand capital gain. In between those two comes the borderline case, and the whole question can only be determined by the courts on the facts as to where that borderline occurs, whether or not a man is engaged in it as a business or whether it was an incidental investment.
Proceeding further, I will not touch on mining now but will deal with it when the next resolution is before the committee. As fairly as possible I tried to portray the difficulty which perfectly respectable private companies find themselves in when it comes to winding up. If they have accumulated a large surplus and do not know what to do with it there is nothing at any time which prevents them from paying dividends out of that surplus. They can do that at any time, and it is their problem. I want to refer now

to another class of private companies, fortunately very small and generally tightly held, which for their own selfish reasons decided during the war, when personal income tax was very high, to pour out just as little as possible in the way of dividends which would of course then be subject to personal income tax. They decided to hold the money back in a reserve in the hope that after the war personal income tax rates would be lower, and then they would pump it out as dividends. Fortunately that has happened very seldom in this country.
Power was given not to the Minister of Finance but to the Minister of National Revenue under section 9 (6) to take action in such cases. Even after a warning was given such companies had the right to state their case. I believe that so far action has been taken in only six cases. As hon. members who follow this type of legislation will realize, after subsection 2 of the resolution is implemented there will have to be substantial changes in the entire section 9 which of course will be apparent to members when they get the bill on first reading. We are not thinking in terms of companies which pile up profits to evade personal income tax but of private companies who have the problem, which I tried to describe in clear terms, of having to accumulate working capital. There is the problem of what they are going to do in the case of involuntary winding up. The hon. member for Moose Jaw, who knows the problems of private companies, says he cannot see any real advantage in this today. All it does is give these companies an opportunity to put themselves in shape against a forced winding up. For example, if tonight while crossing Wellington street on the way home the hon. member were knocked down, I am quite sure his company would be better able to meet the tax on whatever undistributed income his company may have if he chose to take advantage of this resolution-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Take advantage of being knocked down?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -because, having paid this 15 per cent on the undistributed income, the company could be satisfactorily wound up if necessary because of reasons beyond its control, or even within its control.

Then would the parliamentary assistant state categorically that it is not the intention of the government at an early date in future to force companies to get rid of their undistributed profits or surplus?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: Why would they do it? The parliamentary assistant still will not say that in the mind of the Department of Finance, or whoever it is, there is not the idea that they will give us a year to get our house in order and at the end of that time, if we have not done it, we are likely to have undistributed profits taxed substantially.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member is confusing the report of the Ives commission with this resolution. There is no limit of one year here.
All I am asking is whether the government is getting ready to do something next year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend is asking me what is going to be in the budget next year. Hon. members know that even a week before the budget is presented people ask the minister the same question and one can only give them the bland assurance that these matters are under consideration. I cannot tell what is going to be in the budget next year, but in view of the fact that there will be substantial changes in section 9 of the act because of this resolution I would suggest that hon. members wait until the bill is brought down. Then they will have at least a week to study the implications of this resolution with respect to section 9 as it now stands.

Just to go a step further with the happy suggestion of the parliamentary assistant with respect to the hon. member for Moose Jaw, supposing he were knocked down tonight, could his trustees take advantage of this provision after his death?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The answer is that if he had just one trustee that would be possible. If he has more than seventy-five trustees it is without the confines of this resolution.
But it would no longer be a private company then.

When the parliamentary assistant first spoke on this matter he compared this suggested action to the first Ives distribution. I see a considerable difference, in that this is not a distribution; it is a capitalization. I think it should be pointed out that this is not money that will foe distributed to shareholders. Rather it is money that will be capitalized, and cannot be distributed.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is quite correct - in that observation.

Following the questions of the hon. member for Moose Jaw I want to ask the parliamentary assistant this question. You say this simply gives an opportunity to these honest, small companies to put their house in order. To put their house in order against what? Against what the government may do to them if they do do not take advantage of it? Is that what you mean?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
I think that is the only inference one can draw.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The answer is, to get their house in order against involuntary winding up under section 9(1). That is where the problem arises. That is the opportunity they have, if they want to do it. If they do not do this, on winding up the undistributed income is going to be taxed as income of that year and, depending upon the income of the shareholder, it may be taxed at a high rate.

Then we have it clearly that if one pays the 15 per cent now he is free of all further claims with respect to income tax against what may have been undistributed profits, which may have gone into working capital or elsewhere. If that is not done, however, the statement now is that the government will step in and in one year take this surplus, which probably has been accumulated over dozens of years, as profit in that year. Whether the parliamentary assistant realizes it or not, that is what he has just said. I can quite see the fears in the mind of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, that being so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member realizes, of course, that this is the law right now, if a company has to be wound up. What we are trying to do by this resolution is what I attempted to explain in my opening remarks; that is, allow a beneficial option which a man can take but which he does not have to take unless he wishes. If he does take it, then on the winding up of his company he will not be faced with these further difficulties. That is why it is so important to private companies, because death does interfere with the plans of those companies. On winding up, then, they are free from this very heavy penalty under section 9(1) as a result of having the accumulation of years suddenly taxed as the income of one year. If they do not want to take advantage of this option, at least they cannot say they did not have the chance; and as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pointed out, even then their trustee may take advantage of it.

Let us say I
started a little company, made a little money and put it back into machinery or other capital expenditures. Unless I take advantage of this provision, at the end of the road the government comes along and takes all my investment. It can easily amount to that. They could take everything I had invested in my company, though it was in the nature of capital assets which were purchased with earned money, such as machinery and so on. The government could step in and take it all if I did not pay this 15 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not take it all; tax whatever it would amount to as income received in that year.

Let us assume the parliamentary assistant and I have $100,000 in a company. I would have to borrow my $50,000 from you, I know, but we will assume we have that much invested. Of that amount $75,000 is in assets of various kinds, buildings, land, machinery, movable assets and so on. On winding up we must pay income tax on the whole of that, though it is not realizable, and that means the end of the enterprise. That is a situation which may easily arise, is it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Let us make one real distinction. The $100,000 you are speaking of must be in the form of capital equipment acquired by plowing back profits which have not been declared as the personal income of those owning the company. That would not apply to the original capital, or to any further capital which was raised in other ways.
But the company has paid the corporation tax.
During the war years there were no personal taxes on these closely-held companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
But that is the law as it now
stands. Now we are at least giving them the opportunity of paying 15 per cent on that accumulation, if they wish to take advantage of it, which will relieve them of having that money regarded as income in the year of winding up.

The parliamentary assistant is getting us more mixed up as he goes along, and I would like to have this clear before we leave it. Perhaps I am a little more stupid than other hon. members; many may agree with that. Nevertheless I still do not understand the reasoning of the parliamentary assistant in the case of a person dying. If a person dies is it not simply a question of paying death duties, or whatever you call them? Could he not protect himself against

the eventuality that the parliamentary assistant has mentioned by having a substantial insurance policy? I would think that would be the easier way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I quite agree that that is another way if anyone wants to do it. I may point out that if it is a large estate, then the succession duties would be much more than 15 per cent which he would have to pay to clear it in advance. That again is a matter of business choice for the private business concern. Today we are at least giving them some opportunity if they wish-there is nothing forced about it-to put their house in order without taking out insurance.
Is the parliamentary assistant suggesting that a man must first pay succession duties, and then pay income tax or whatever you want to call it on the surplus-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, I am wrong on that, it is income tax.
He has to pay income tax on his surplus then, on top of that, succession duties?

In other words, Mr. Chairman, a man can be very successful in his business while he is alive, but when he dies he may leave nothing but a cause for battle between the succession duty people and the income tax people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Getting back to the hon. member's question, I unfortunately used the phrase "succession duties". The succession duties would have to be paid on the capital, but under section 9(1) of the act as at present that portion which goes to his estate in the form of undistributed income is regarded as income for that year, and would be subject to income tax according to the level of his income at the rates for that year, in exactly the same way as earned dividends.
All that he has built up over a period of years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, so today we are giving him this beneficial provision, so that rather than face up to that, he can put his house in order by paying the 15 per cent.

The successful way of dealing with this matter would be by repealing this section 9(1), if that is the case. In spite of all that the parliamentary assistant has said, it still looks to me as though next year the government is planning to bring in a tax on undistributed income if they take advantage of this 15 per cent clause. Nothing the parliamentary assistant has said has dispelled that fear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I certainly do not intend to attempt to forecast what the government is
Income Tax Act
going to do in its budget program a year from now. I would suggest that if we repealed section 9(1), then no company would ever pay any dividends. The dividends would be salted away, and then when a firm wound up all of that profit would be capital, and income tax payments would have been avoided.
They can be caught today without that clause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I tried to point out earlier, because of the points that have been mentioned by the member for Eglinton, the member for Moose Jaw and the member for London, it is quite obvious that there will be substantial changes in section 9 (1) when the bill is brought down.

It seems to me that this is an entirely new principle and a dangerous one. A shareholder in a private company, that is a company with less than seventy-five shareholders, may own 15 per cent of the shares of the company. Throughout the years the company may be able to build up through profits an undistributed surplus of say $100,000. The company in its wisdom plans to use that $100,000 at some time in the future for a project it plans to undertake when the time is propitious. The shareholder owning 15 per cent of that company dies. Under this regulation the surplus in that company which was built up, or at least 15 per cent of it, is considered taxable in the year of death as income.
Surely, that is an entirely new principle. The shareholder has the option of paying 15 per cent of what he may expect the surplus in the company to be, or have his share of the undivided surplus regarded as income in the year of his death. Surely that is a new principle and a wrong principle. It is the principle of a capital gains tax written right into the act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Once again I shall try to spell it out. This company has accumulated $100,000 as a surplus. If this company had paid out of its profits each year the full dividends, the shareholder receiving those each year would have paid personal income tax which begins at 15 per cent over exemption. However, for good reasons which I tried to outline, the company has accumulated the $100,000. Now, not under legislation proposed but under existing legislation passed by this parliament, section 9(1) of this act says that the $100,000, representing accumulated profits which have not been pumped out and have not been subject to personal income tax when spread around the shareholders, is taxable when the company is wound up.

Income Tax Act
Using this example, out of the dividend which is taxable as income, the shareholder's $15,000 would be taxable at income tax rates for his category. Let us suppose the company took advantage of this proposal and paid 15 per cent. The company would then have $85,000 to distribute tax free. That would be his, instead of having to pay at his personal income tax rate on the $15,000. In that case it is obviously beneficial to that man if his company takes advantage of this proposal.

But that is in the case of a company being wound up. I am speaking of the case of the death of a minority shareholder while the company is still in business and proposes to carry on business. It has $100,000 of a surplus, and the man who dies has 15 per cent of the stock. His stock is sold, and it appears to me that under this proposal his estate would be liable. I am glad to see the minister shaking his head. It seems to me his estate would be liable under this clause for the tax on the surplus, whether or not it had been distributed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I pointed out that the application of this clause is on the winding up of a company. If the stock of the shareholder who dies can be sold, he is in exactly the same position as the shareholder of a public company who can sell stock. The normal processes continue after that. It is only because of the special financial problems in these closely held companies, when the principal shareholder dies and the company has to be wound up, that this clause is needed. If the ordinary shareholder dies and his stock can be sold, then the position is no different from one who holds stock in a large corporation whose shares have a market value. This section is only applicable on the winding up which is a problem that arises principally because of the death of the one who holds controlling interest in a small company. Then, not only the heirs of the person who died, but the persons who are left in the company, are forced to accept this distribution as soon as the company has been wound up. I think you have followed the illustration I gave. It is obviously to the advantage of the shareholder, in the example the hon. member put forward, to have this tax paid, but there again it is a matter of choice.

I should like to ask a question. It may not be in order. If it is not in order the parliamentary assistant may say so. Suppose an individual, or a private company, bought a block of land and timber. He does not take a timber lease; he buys the land and all. Of course he buys it on the instalment

basis and pays so much each year. It takes every dollar he can make and scrape together to make his payments, which he must show as income. He pays income tax on it every year until he has probably 75 per cent or 80 per cent of the timber cut off, on which he has also paid income tax. He still holds the land and a certain amount of timber that he could take off if he wishes, which would pay for the land. On this land he has some lake property. He wishes to develop that lake-shore property and sell it for lots, but not individual lots. Does he have to pay income tax on the return from that land?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the hon. member's case comes down to this-[DOT] I find it quite difficult to follow it through-if he has bought a block of land for timber purposes, and part of it he later sold, that would be an ordinary capital gain and would not be subject to tax. If on the other hand he is a real estate promotor and does that all the time, then his income from that in that year is going to be taxable as income.

Just one other question to sum this thing up. I want to make sure that I clearly understand it. Do I take it that resolution 2 is an insurance policy which a man can buy for 15 per cent of his surplus and protect his family from a much larger tax in case he dies? Is that all it is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is pretty well the intent of this bill. That accurately sums it up. Once having paid the tax he has this tax-paid surplus, as far as the winding up is concerned, when this undistributed income is going to be distributed among the shareholders.

Will the parliamentary
assistant state whether the treasury board discussed it at meetings which he attended? Did they discuss whether or not, if businessmen did not put their house in order, as he suggested, this year, next year there would be a substantial change in the budget?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To begin with, I am not a member of treasury board.
But you attend its meetings.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I occasionally attend. Whether I attend or not, there is obviously a pledge of secrecy as to what goes on there, so I could not tell the hon. member in any case. Getting back once again to the question, nobody here is able to forecast what is to be in the budget a year from now. That is why, as hon. members all know, there is intense interest in the budget. Anyway, all I can say is that this is the program of the government, and when the bill is brought down and the hon. member gives his usual studious care to section 9 he

will find the appropriate changes being made to accommodate this resolution with the present section 9 of the Income Tax Act.

There is one remark that the parliamentary assistant made a few moments ago that calls for some comment. It will be remembered that when I was speaking earlier I read a Canadian Press dispatch, giving the date of it, and mentioning that it appeared in a number of Canadian newspapers, in which extended remarks were attributed to a so-called "government spokesman." That expression appeared in the press article several -times. I invited the parliamentary assistant, or someone speaking on behalf of the government, to disclaim any policy of the kind that was announced in the article. In his reply the parliamentary assistant began first of all by accusing me of quoting something without disclosing the source. Apparently he had quite overlooked that I had said that it was a Canadian Press dispatch, and appeared under a Canadian Press byline. I gave the date and mentioned that it appeared in various Canadian newspapers. In addition to that, without actually making the kind of statement that I invited him or someone speaking for the government to make, indicating to us that the kind of policy outlined in that article was not and is not government policy, he chose to berate any who would suggest that articles appearing in that form, attributed to a so-called "government spokesman," were in fact a form of government release, and said that when government releases were to be made they would be made by ministers, and they would make statements. I do not propose to let that remark pass unchallenged, sir, because every member in this house knows perfectly well that when the government wishes to pass out some publicity, to make a statement without committing itself too far to it, or to fly a trial balloon, they simply put out, through one of their multitude of publicity men in the various departments, one of these statements to -the press, and the remarks are attributed to a government spokesman.
You had a very good example this afternoon, sir, of just the way in which the government abuses this method of publicity.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what you think.	'

That is what I am telling the minister; and if the article I read this afternoon does not reflect government policy, sir, then I invite the Minister of Public Works to rise in his place and say right now that that article does not represent government policy and never did. Second, I invite the minister-
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only answer I can give-
to say that that article-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You would not stop for an answer.

I will give the minister ample opportunity in a minute, Mr. Chairman. Second, I invite him to say that that article, ascribed to a government spokesman, was not in fact authorized by any government department or any government official who had power and authority to issue such a statement. If he will do that I shall have some other interesting questions to ask him, either now or on another occasion.
The minister knows perfectly well, sir, and every hon. member knows perfectly well, the way in which the government abuses this practice. If they get something which they think is good-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is all good.

-which they think will be popular, then, of course, the minister will make the statement and will take the responsibility or credit for it. If they think it may not be so popular, if they want to test public opinion, then of course the statement is ascribed to "a government spokesman." I am making this point perfectly clear this afternoon. I am not going to debate this matter further. When the parliamentary assistant this afternoon undertakes to say that the statement reproduced by the Canadian Press, and ascribed to a so-called government spokesman, is not equivalent to a government release, then he is just flying in the face of the facts. As every hon. member knows perfectly well, the Canadian Press would not take that statement and publish it in this form unless it -came from an accredited government source. If that is the way in which the government is using all these expenditures on publicity which we discussed recently, then I think it is high time-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I hope we are not
going to get away from what is under discussion. My hon. friend is just building up straw men by suggesting that when the government decides on a policy it needs someone else to announce it. I say to the hon. member that when the government decides on a policy there are enough ministers to make the announcement, and that is the way in which we proceed. If you will just keep to what is under discussion, and let the other questions that you have in mind come up in due course, they will be discussed.

Income Tax Act
It is quite obvious that the minister was not in the house when the press dispatch was read.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am here quite often.
I say this to the minister also: We are discussing the budget resolutions now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which one?

I was speaking a moment ago of subjects that were discussed in the budget debate, and which are properly before the committee now. If the minister had been in the house he would not attempt to suggest that this matter is not properly before the committee, because the parliamentary assistant has undertaken to challenge this particular press release as being something authorized on behalf of the government.
Now, sir, I am leaving the subject with this parting observation, that it is a pretty fair sample of the way the government plays fast and loose with publicity they put out; and we can ask ourselves at the proper time whether very heavy expenditures for government publicity in all departments are warranted at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers when we see this abuse made of such publicity on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot let this pass unchallenged. The hon. member is very excited now, as he generally is when he gets worked up. He has left the inference that the Canadian Press was the publicity agent of the government. The government will make their announcements with regard to policy in due course, and the ministers will make the statements, as my minister did in the budget speech. But the hon. member is naive when he makes the suggestion that a minister should get up and immediately deny any kite flown by the press, because-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Or the opposition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Or the opposition-they want to lead these hard-working gentlemen of the press up some blind alley and fly a kite, because they want to challenge the government to put out government policy in advance. Any statement of policy from the Department of Finance will come from the Minister of Finance, and he need not rely upon unauthorized government spokesmen in press dispatches.

Will the parliamentary assistant answer this question simply-because I asked it when I first spoke, if he would say this, or if someone would-will he say that the press dispatch from which I read does not reflect government policy?
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member must think I am more naive than most people. I have just tried to explain-and I am sure other hon. members who were not all heated up were listening-that it would be an easy way to find out future government policy to have the press fly a kite, and then get up and demand that the government either deny or accept this press release.

Supposing for the moment that we have done with the article. As an innocent member I am asking a simple question of the parliamentary assistant. I say, regardless of whether it was a government spokesman or not to whom this statement of policy is ascribed, will the parliamentary assistant answer a simple question, yes or no, as to whether the policy outlined in that article is or is not government policy? It is a simple question; a yes or no answer would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Government policy today, so far as taxation is concerned, is governed by the present Income Tax Act. When the new act is brought down the hon. member will be able to know what new government policy therfe is, so far as taxation is concerned.

That is not an answer at all. To call that an answer would be just to insult the intelligence of a schoolboy. If the parliamentary assistant desires to make any progress, then I suggest that instead of ranting, as he has been doing, and thrashing the air with his arms he accept my invitation on that subject we were discussing as to forcing the distribution of corporate surpluses, to say whether that newspaper article-and he must be familiar with it by now

does or does not reflect government policy. It is so simple it could be answered yes or no.
I make it clear to the parliamentary assistant that I do not propose to be given the run-around on my question. It is a simple question, it is relevant to the subject under discussion, and if the parliamentary assistant wishes to give information and wishes to expedite the proceedings it will permit of his giving a very simple answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, once again, these resolutions are to give the intent, and either decrease or increase the tax, and the change in regulations which cover any changes in legislation. The present act provides, in section 9(6), that the minister, in his discretion, has this right, which has apparently been used six times. As to whether or not that right, which is not the sort of material covered by the resolution, will be changed, the hon. member will find out when the new act, with the new section 9, is brought down

for first reading. And when that first reading takes place will depend, of course, on how long the hon. member wishes to talk.
The parliamentary assistant is dodging a simple question. We came here this afternoon prepared to be thoroughly co-operative and to obtain necessary information.
Oh, oh.

Yes, we have been thoroughly co-operative. If the parliamentary assistant wishes to give the information, in reply to a simple question, then we will proceed very much more quickly than by having some hon. members opposite-and I sympathize with them, because they do not get a chance to do anything else-murmur in undertones. We will progress faster if the parliamentary assistant will give the information, which is of a very proper and relevant nature-and it is simple, quite simple. I have asked him what is government policy. We have had a statement as to what purports to be government policy. Surely in the face of that it would be competent for the parliamentary assistant to say yes or no, as to whether that is government policy. And if he does not know, then we shall accept a frank answer to that effect, and we shall ask the Minister of Finance-or the Minister of Public Works, who has undertaken to speak for the government on this occasion, I believe. We will ask him to give the information.
I am not going to pick and choose among the ministers. I would just as soon have the Minister of Public Works answer a financial question as any other minister-the Minister of Finance included. I am sure he knows as much about problems of finance in government as any government minister. So I should be very happy if the minister will answer my simple, straightforward, proper and relevant question-if, for the first time in his life, the parliamentary assistant is tongue-tied:

I am always interested in any change or alteration in the English language. I think probably one of the functions of parliament is to call attention to any new usage. On behalf of the committee I should like to inform those who prepare Webster's dictionary that from now on "government spokesman" means "journalist's balloon".

In connection with a company which has built up a surplus of $100,000 over a period of years and decides to invest that money in an extension of plant: if I own 75 per cent of the stock of the company and die before the act comes into effect,
Income Tax Act
what happens? Are my heirs assessed on the amount of that stock, that surplus, at 100 per cent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In the case the hon. member

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is a very interesting section. Again it is brought on by some of the problems of financing these days. I will use the example of a chain store which after all is in the business of buying and selling food. Some of them do not want their capital tied up unnecessarily in real estate, the property they have to buy and the parking space next door. Therefore the practice has developed of some of these institutions, such as chain stores or service stations, selling their properties for a capital sum to an insurance company and then leasing it back under an annual hire purchase agreement. For example, $100,000 is the value of the property. They pay $20,000 for five years, and at the end by a payment of a small sum, $1 or $100, they acquire the property. They may hope of course that the payment of $100,000 will be regarded as rent of the property and therefore deductible as an operating cost of doing business.
Of course that rate would be very much higher, than the depreciation on a firm down the street owning a similar property and taking the ordinary depreciation allowed under the law. More than that, if the land is included in that they are actually in effect getting depreciation on land which of course is not allowed under ordinary depreciation schedules. Of course many of these deals are perfectly bona fide. The longer the'term of the lease the more closely it approaches ordinary depreciation rates. The present act applies this principle to movable property. Now we are extending it a little further and applying it to immovable property as well, other than that used in farming.

While I understand the explanation, I wonder why this clause has been put in at the end, "except real or immovable property used in the business of farming." Although this provision apparently was put in there to cover the chain stores people and so on, it would apply to everybody except farmers. Why are they specifically exempted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand my hon. friend comes from a farming riding and I am a little surprised that he should raise that question. I believe he is a farmer himself.
I am asking for an explanation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: , One reason is that last year farmers were allowed to continue taking straight-line depreciation if they so wished. On the other hand, everybody else, other than farmers and fishermen, must take diminishing balance in which there is a recapture provision. That is one reason why farmers are excluded.

This section says that such agreements are deemed to be agreements for sale and the payments to be purchase price. In other words, in such contracts as are mentioned in this section no allowance is to be made for the deduction of any interest that may be involved in the payment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Interest is regarded as a part of the purchase price in that the purchase price is spread over these periods.

The parliamentary assistant has just raised a question about interest and has said that under these hire-purchase agreements interest is to be regarded in effect as a part of the purchase price. This situation has wider involvements and implications, and I think the committee should pause a moment to consider them.
In the Income Tax Act we have provision made for the deduction of interest on borrowed money used to earn the income of the taxpayer. To most people there should not be any difference between cases A and B. In case A the individual taxpayer, being possessed of a certain asset-it may be of the kind referred to in the resolution, the purchase of some equipment-in the course of his operations goes out, borrows money and pays interest on the money borrowed. In case A if the money is borrowed and used in the course of earning the income of the taxpayer then he will be allowed that interest by way of deduction as a business expense. But take the case of the taxpayer B who purchases some equipment, either under a hire-purchase agreement or subject to an existing encumbrance. Suppose he buys property, it may be either real or personal, subject to a first and second mortgage, or perhaps a third mortgage. If he simply assumes existing obligations and pays interest on those obligations, the taxing authorities of this country say they will not grant him any deduction in respect of his payment of interest on account of encumbrances existing when he bought the property.
That is an extraordinary situation, and I wish to express my regret that something has not been done in these resolutions to 55946-1381
Income Tax Act
eliminate that anomaly, which is very discriminatory in its operations. An eminent writer on the subject of income tax asked this question recently in a well known publication:
If a company buys a building for $100,000, assumes a $50,000 first mortgage and gives a $30,000 second mortgage, it has not borrowed the $50,000 nor the $30,000-
He is speaking now of the interpretation by our taxing authorities.
-and, therefore, cannot charge the interest on these amounts as an expense.
Or if a taxpayer agrees to pay $10,000 for a piece of plant, payable $1,000 down and $1,000 a month with interest, he cannot charge the interest as expense. Why? Because he did not borrow the money first and then pay off the $10,000 at once. If he had done so the interest would have been allowed.
Must all the modern methods of buying assets be revised in order not to have the interest disallowed under this decision?
This very directly affects the farmer. Here is a situation that came to my attention not long ago. Attention is drawn here to an extraordinary tax situation under which a farmer who would purchase machinery and borrow money to pay for it is permitted to charge interest on the borrowed money as a business expense, while the farmer who buys machinery on deferred payments cannot deduct interest on the balance as a business expense; and the same thing applies to other purchases of capital goods.
The income tax appeal board has ruled that a man who bought a garage for $50,000, of which $10,000 was declared to be interest, should be refused permission to treat this as a business expense. If he had borrowed the money from some third party and purchased the garage for cash, he would have been entitled to treat the interest on the loan as a business expense.
That situation just reeks with anomaly. I 'do not think anyone could defend it as common sense. I must express regret that apparently nothing is proposed to meet that situation.
I refer to the decision in the McCool case by the Supreme Court of Canada last year. The full title is Minister of National Revenue
u.	T. E. McCool Limited, reported at 49 Canadian Tax Cases, page 395. In that case a situation of this kind came before the Supreme Court of Canada for interpretation; and what I have indicated in my remarks up to the moment is the interpretation that the Supreme Court of Canada placed upon section 5(1) of the Income War Tax Act, which in this respect is in terms similar to section 11(1) (c>
of the Income Tax Act. In effect what the Supreme Court of Canada said in that case was that before the money regarded as being

Income Tax Act
an obligation upon the taxpayer would be treated as a loan under that section of the act, so that the amount paid by way of interest on the loan would be considered by the Department of National Revenue as a business expense, there must be a real loan and a real borrower. That is the language used in this report, and I am referring now to the judgment of Mr. Justice Kellock at page 407. Then Mr. Justice Kellock went on to say:
Here there is nothing more than unpaid purchase money secured by a promissory note which, in my opinion, is insufficient.
In that case the encumbrance had existed prior to the purchase by the taxpayer, and he was not permitted to treat what he had to pay on that money by way of interest as an expense. Then Mr. Justice Kellock goes on to say:
It is not sufficient to say that if the company had borrowed the amount of the note and paid McCool it would have been entitled to the deduction. However that may be, that was not done and the statute does not apply.
Then at page 413, after quoting the terms of section 5(1) (b) of the Income War Tax Act in relation to the interest on borrowed capital, Mr. Justice Estey said:
Terms such as "borrowed capital" "borrowed money" in tax legislation have been interpreted to mean capital or money borrowed with a relationship of lender and borrower between the parties. It is necessary in determining whether that relationship exists to ascertain the true nature and character of the transaction. In this case the promissory note arises out of an exchange in which, as already detailed, the purchase price was paid by assuming outstanding obligations, a small payment of cash, allotment of capital stock and the execution and delivering of this promissory note. Under such circumstances it cannot be held that the relationship of lender and borrower in respect to this note exists between the respondent company and the payee of the note.
That decision has been followed in at least one other case since, the Rhinehorne case, recently decided in the exchequer court.. This is a situation which I believe demands immediate redress. It offends the ordinary common sense of all people to say that if a man buys subject to existing obligations and as part of the purchase price assumes those obligations and agrees to pay interest on them, and after completing the purchase goes on to pay the interest, he shall not be entitled to regard that as interest on borrowed money and therefore as a business expense, while at the same time if that man made an outright purchase without assuming obligations or encumbrances, and borrowed capital afterwards for use in the course of his business, for the purpose of earning an income, the interest on that borrowed capital may be deducted from his income as a business expense.
[Mr. Fleming.l
Under those conditions I say it offends against common sense to say that in their result the two cases should be absolutely and diametrically opposite in the view of the taxing authorities. For the purposes of that taxpayer the situation to all intents and purposes is the same, but the result for taxation purposes is exactly the opposite. This is going to affect a great many farmers and businessmen in this country, and I urge that the matter should receive immediate attention by the government in order that remedial legislation may be brought down. The proper remedy, of course, is not to deny to the taxpayer in the latter case the right to regard that payment of interest as an expense. The proper remedy is to permit the taxpayer in the former case to treat the payment of interest on obligations he has assumed as an expense within the terms of section 5 of the Income War Tax Act, or section 11(1) (c) of the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member will be very glad to learn that the supreme court decision has been brought to the attention of the government and remedial legislation will be brought down in the bill that will be introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Before it is called six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I see we have made some progress this afternoon and we may get through with these resolutions some 
time during the evening. Last night I announced we would take up resolution No. 3 on the order paper, that is the amendment to the Research Council Act to appoint one more vice-president; that is not very lengthy. Then, I announced we would take up the resolution of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. This is a continuation of that matter, and there have already been fifteen speakers, so I do not think that will take very long.
I would suggest, in all fairness to the house, that if we complete those things before eleven we have three small bills with which we might deal, and I shall name them. One is the act respecting the appointment of the auditors for the Canadian National Railways. The second is the bill to amend the Manitoba Boundaries Extension Act, 1912, and the Ontario Boundaries Extension Act. I understand both provinces have passed statutes concerning the boundary, and they need a bill here to approve those things. There is a third bill, No. 18 on today's order paper, an act to amend the Department of Transport Stores Act. I understand the purpose of the bill is to increase the revolving fund, and to find a way of declaring obsolete a portion of the stores that they have on hand.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I want to make a few remarks on this resolution, but I should like to ask a question of the parliamentary assistant in order to make one point clear. Could he tell me why the Geneva agreements, which were formulated about three years ago, have not yet been passed by parliament? Is there a special reason why?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not only have they not been passed by this parliament, but so far as I am aware no other parliament of the signatory countries has yet passed them. As hon. members know, the Geneva agreements have been continued by further discussions at Annecy, and are now going to be further discussed at Torquay this summer. What we are doing as fast as we can is implementing actually in our legislation the undertakings given at Geneva, and these amendment changes are almost entirely because of the Geneva trade agreements.

Mr. Chairman, in a general way, as far as these customs tariff amendments now before us are concerned, this group is disappointed that the government has not

seen fit at this time to proceed with further tariff reductions, particularly against British goods.
The parliamentary assistant and other hon. members will bear in mind that on numerous occasions over the past several years this group has asked in parliament that tariffs be lowered against British goods, so that the British might earn dollars to buy our merchandise, our farm products, and the like. I must say that I am getting just a little bit tired of listening to my goods friends in the Liberal party, in parliament and out of parliament, preach about the need for freer trade, for fewer restrictions, for lower tariffs, while they do so little about them.
The resolutions in front of us today are, in my opinion, a good example of that lack of action. For several years the Minister of Finance has argued in his budget speeches about the need for lower tariff barriers. And he has always admitted the need to help Britain sell more goods in this country. But every time he comes to parliament he has the same excuse for inaction. His reason for inaction last year is to be found at page 1801 of Hansard. He said:
In view of the pending tariff negotiations at Annecy and other trade discussions which are envisaged, and in view also of the intention to introduce legislation at a later date to implement the general agreement on tariffs and trade, I am not proposing any tariff changes at the present time.
Well, a month or so later he brought down the Annecy agreements, but I am sure even the most ardent member of the government would not say that these were particularly significant changes. Then this year the minister had another reason for not doing very much about the tariff schedules, and I quote from his budget speech at page 1218 of Hansard:
In view of the important tariff negotiations which are scheduled to commence in a few months' time-
He refers to Torquay.
-the budget resolutions relating to the customs tariff which I am tabling contain very few changes.
I say this very respectfully. In my opinion the Minister of Finance is possibly one of the best exponents of double talk in this House of Commons. In his budget speech last year he said it was government policy to help British exporters regain their historic share of the Canadian market; and yet in his next breath he announced the reimposition of tariffs against British textiles. Look at his budget speech again this year. He went on for five or ten minutes at page 1218 of Hansard, if I remember correctly, to speak about the need of lowering tariffs. Yet on page 1219, a minute later, he announced an increase of 15 per cent in the tariff against British tinplate. I ask the parliamentary assistant to explain
Customs Tariff
where there is consistency in these words. I ask him to give us more information as to why such a change was necessary.
Today, Mr. Chairman, two-thirds of Canadian exports are going to the United States. That fact is a cause for some satisfaction, but it is also a cause for considerable concern, because since the end of the war Canada has been seeing her usual and traditional markets in Britain, the commonwealth and Europe, shrink. The fact that we have been able to make up for these losses in the United States is probably an achievement. Yet at the same time we are subject to that old danger which often happens when we put all our eggs in one basket. It seems to me that this is what we are doing with our export trade today. The United States is by no means the most stable market in the world. Our past experience bears that out; because overnight, in the past, United States tariff changes have virtually wiped out our markets. An economic recession in the United States has had a similar effect. Therefore I say that since we are selling two-thirds of our exports in the United States we are vulnerable to several things-first, a change in the United States administration; second, a change in their tariff policy, and third, to economic conditions in the United States if they become worse. In view of the vulnerable position which I have pointed out, Mr. Chairman, I think that when the Canadian delegation goes to Torquay in a few months' time they must go there with that in mind.
I was interested in an article which appeared in the Financial Post about a week ago. It was written by Kenneth Wilson. I should like to quote it:
A new battle over what's left of the empire preferential tariff system now looms for 1950-51 as 40 nations begin preparations for the full-dress trade negotiations scheduled for Torquay, England, next September.
Canada has very few important preferences left to negotiate. But United Kingdom and empire preferences in the Canadian market are still substantial.
These will be under heavy attack at Torquay, especially by European countries.
I am one who believes in freer trade, but I am also one who believes that we should guard these commonwealth preferential tariffs with a degree of care.
It seems to me that diverse markets are safer markets. Any action which would further increase our economic dependence upon the United States at this time is, in my view, to be viewed with concern. It is possible that the government may make a grievous mistake if it goes to Torquay and agrees to scrap commonwealth preference.

Customs Tariff
I think, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's No. 1 trade problem is still to regain our markets in Europe, to regain our commonwealth markets, to regain our markets in Britain. British leaders have told us repeatedly that there is only one way to do that, namely, to let them sell more in this country so that they can earn Canadian dollars. One of my criticisms of the customs tariff regulations which are now before us is that the government has been apathetic in this respect. The government has been lax in watching the British buyers gradually choked out of the Canadian market through their lack of dollars. If our main problem so far as tariffs is concerned is to get back some of these commonwealth markets, then I view with concern certain tendencies which seem to me to be prevalent in this country. Protectionists of various kinds seem to be more active. Not so long ago dumping duties were applied against certain Japanese textiles, I read in the newspapers that interests in British Columbia in the cement business are asking for dumping duties against Japanese cement. I heard this afternoon in the house, I believe it was the hon. member for Norfolk, ask for protection against strawberry pulp coming from Holland. These applications are bad enough, but there is one which should concern this house in particular. At page 1904 of Hansard I asked the Minister of National Revenue whether or not any application had been received for dumping duties against small English cars, and his answer was, "Yes." I then asked him what disposal had been made of such requests, and he answered, "The matter is under consideration." Mr. Chairman, I am amazed that a government which professes to believe in freer trade would consider for more than ten minutes such a high-handed request, because for several years our government has been urging British manufacturers to get their prices down and to become competitive, so that they can sell in this market. Apparently the British automobile manufacturers have been successful in doing that because they are able to bring their cars here, pay freight on them, pay sales tax and still compete.
Now, the automobile manufacturers, I presume, want dumping duty protection. I would remind the government of two things: first that Canadian cheap cars have roughly doubled in price since 1939, and secondly, that the Canadian automobile industry today has almost complete protection from American competition, (a) because of the tariff, (b) because of exchange differences and (c) because of import quotas. There is virtually no American competition, so far as Canadian cars are concerned.

Therefore I say that the request, whomever it is from, a short sighted, narrow-minded request made on the basis of self-interest. If Canadian automobiles are entitled to dumping duty protection, or to additional tariff protection, whichever you choose to call it, then every other industry in Canada in a similar position is entitled to the same protection.
Of course, if that protection were brought in, it is obvious what would happen to our trade with Great Britain. The whole proposition I say is absurd. If the Canadian automobile industry want to sell more cars in Canada, then let them get their prices down. Let them compete. I am sure the average Canadian consumer would welcome such a decrease in the cost of living.
Mr. Chairman, I refer to all pressure cases of this kind. I think they come at a most inopportune time-coming as they do a few months before the free nations of the world meet at Torquay to discuss eliminating trade restrictions and lowering tariffs generally. I think there are few things that would darken the prospects at Torquay as much as Canada's coming forward with further protectionist measures at this time.
This nation has to depend for its prosperity upon lower tariffs and upon fewer restrictions. To raise barriers just before an international effort to lower them would be, in my opinion, an act of economic folly. I hope the parliamentary assistant will give more information about these dumping duties. What is the policy of the government going to be in future? I wish he would give some assurance to the people of Canada that, so far as British automobiles are concerned, there is not going to be the imposition of any dumping duty.
In conclusion I wish to urge the government once again to translate some of its lofty words in the house and elsewhere about freer trade into some concrete action. Hon. members in this group realize, I think, as do members in other groups, that upon freer trade rests the best assurance for Canada to avoid a recession in the immediate future.

Before the parliamentary assistant replies I should like to second the comments of the hon. member for Moose Jaw with respect to these tariffs. There is just one further point I would bring to the attention of the committee, and that is a point which is brought out in the Auditor General's report. At page 11 we find in section 39 the heading, "Tariff items and customs drawback", and it states:
The governor in council may, from time to time, and in the manner hereinafter provided, in addition to the other purposes and matters in this act mentioned, make regulations for or relating to the following purposes and matters:

(1)	granting a drawback of the whole or part of the duty paid on articles which have been used in Canadian manufactures, or granting a certain specific sum in lieu of any such drawback.
And then at page 12 we find the Auditor General's comment with respect to P.C. 4793 passed by the governor in council on October 22, 1948-
-providing drawback of 99 per cent of customs duty paid on certain imported steel sheets, when used in the manufacture of stampings for automobiles.
Here we have a case where the government is giving a 99 per cent drawback to the manufacturers of automobiles in this country on certain types of steel being imported into Canada. At the same time the manufacturers come to the government asking for dumping duties on English cars, when they have American cars completely barred from the market. I am asking the parliamentary assistant what protection the buyers of cars have in this country. Who is getting the benefit of this 99 per cent drawback the manufacturer is getting on customs duties in connection with the steel used for the stampings going into the manufacture of cars in this country? It certainly is not the buyer, when we find that the same car, exactly, is selling for $400 or $500 more than it is in the United States, while at the same time the workman in the United States factory is receiving from 30 to 40 per cent more in wages than is the man doing the same work in the Canadian factory.
When the governor in council passed this order in council giving the drawback of this duty, what action was taken to see that that drawback is passed on to the Canadian consumer in the price of the goods the manufacturer makes out of the article on which he has received the drawback?

speechtext:
I shall deal first with the points raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. He has asked why we do not make further reduction in the British tariff at the present time. Under the Geneva trade agreements any reductions we now give the British we have also to give to all the other signatory nations. That is the basic principle of the *entire Geneva agreement. We certainly are not going to do that until we have reciprocal concessions from them. That is another reason why we are not making any of these concessions before the meeting at Torquay. It is easy to ask these concessions for other countries, but I think industry in this country is also entitled to some reciprocal arrangement to assist them.
The next point, so far as the British tariff is concerned, is a most interesting one. The figures I gave earlier this afternoon show to what extent we have opened the door to the

British. Last year our total imports from British countries were valued at $504 million of which $321 million, or over three-fifths, were exempt from customs duty. I think that is a pretty fair break, so far as the British market is concerned.
Then, the next point: so far as cars are concerned, British cars enter today free from customs duty. American cars are subject to-

And also a sales tax on Canadian cars. I do not think anyone would say that British cars should be sold in this country and not pay the same tax in that way as do Canadian cars. We put them all on the same footing in this country as our Canadian cars. American cars, on the other hand, pay a duty of 17 per cent on admission to Canada.
The next point he mentioned was that of tinplate. I should like to make a special reference to tinplate when discussing resolution 3. This is the only item since 1936 on which we have raised a tariff; and when the actual reasons are given, and when the figures are known, hon. members will realize how inconsequential it is.
Then there is the matter of the alarm raised by the hon. member because the government has given consideration to a proposal put forward by an industry in this country. I hope that day will never come when the government will not be willing to listen to the representations put forward by any industry, whether it accepts them or not. Of course the automobile industry, like every other industry in Canada-like the farmers in Canada and the fishermen in Canada-would naturally like to have special protection for their industry. When these requests are put forward the government has to give them full consideration and then, in due time, announce a policy with regard to them.
The last point was the one raised by the hon. member for Melfort with respect to this drawback on drawn steel used in the manufacture of stampings for automobiles. This item has been in the tariff since 1930, making provision for steel sheets, hot or cold rolled, or coated with lead or with lead and tin, -064 inch to -032 inch in thickness, 20 to 42 inches in width and 50 to 120 inches in length, if imported and used in the manufacture of stampings for automobiles, giving a 99 per cent drawback. The reason is that at that time we did not manufacture such sizes. The only change that has been made is made because of a difference in design. I am informed that because of the extra width of the present bumpers and fenders on the new cars these coated steel plates are now allowed

Customs Tariff
in from twenty to fifty inches rather than the previous widths of twenty to forty-two inches and fifty to one hundred inches. That is the only difference in a tariff item which has been in effect since 1930.
As far as these drawbacks are concerned, naturally when a drawback is allowed the saving should go on down to the consumer. If the drawback was not allowed then I imagine the consumer buying that car would have to pay for the duty as well. Apparently what caused the comment by the Auditor General was that the change to increase the width of the plates from forty-two to fifty inches to provide for the extra length of bumpers was done by order in council.

I should like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant a matter which is of importance to a large number of Canadians. I have been interested in the fact that there has been a 20 per cent duty against penicillin since some time in 1947. I asked the following question about this some time ago:
1.	Has a tariff been imposed on penicillin? If so, what is the rate of such tariff and when was it first given effect?
The answer received from the Department of National Revenue was as follows:
Yes. The present rate of 20 per cent M.F.N. has been in effect since April 1, 1947.
My second question was:
What was the value of penicillin imported into Canada for the years 1945-46-47-48-49?
The answer by the Department of Trade and Commerce was as follows:
Penicillin was not separately classified in Canadian trade statistics prior to January 1, 1949. Imports of penicillin and products during the calendar year 1949 were valued at $1,507,456.
We are charging a 20 per cent duty on a very necessary drug while under the third resolution to amend the Excise Tax Act we are providing for the removal of the sales tax from a number of articles and materials used by bona fide public institutions certified to be such by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I heartily agree with that because we are doing something commendable to reduce the cost of hospital administration and expense.
I do suggest that it is most unfortunate that we should continue to impose this 20 per cent customs duty on a necessary drug

like penicillin. In going over the schedule at the back of these resolutions I find that there is a 20 per cent tariff against rough granite and a 25 per cent tariff against bagpipes. As far as I am concerned you could put 100 per cent on bagpipes and take it off penicillin. I notice that castor oil comes in free.
When you consider the customs tariff it is hard to see the logic of some of these items. When the parliamentary assistant answers my question I should like him to explain the 25 per cent duty on bagpipes and the 20 per cent duty on penicillin.
Penicillin is used to fight infection, and in this connection it has been used with great success in recent years. It is good for colds, pneumonia, bone diseases and other infections with which hon. members may be familiar.
I am informed by my doctor that where a patient is suffering from pneumonia he may require five or six injections daily for as long as three weeks at a cost of about $5 per day. The 20 per cent tariff on penicillin is an added burden on people who are sick and who can ill afford to pay the cost of this drug.
I should like to know the amount of penicillin manufactured in Canada and why this 20 per cent tariff is placed on such a necessary drug. I should like the parliamentary assistant to use his influence to have this duty on penicillin removed and thus lower the cost of medical treatment, just as we are doing under resolution No. 3 to amend the Excise Tax Act.

I do not rise to defend bagpipes, as some people might expect I would. Even though there might be a 100 per cent duty against bagpipes coming in, they will still flourish. I support what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said. I think it is a shame that people should have to pay a duty on penicillin. I am not talking about this from a medical point of view; I am talking as one who has had to pay for it. I had to pay for it for twenty-seven weeks and when you have poor people like myself in that position it is quite a drag on them. From what doctors tell me this appears to be one of the finest things ever discovered. I join with the hon. member who has just spoken in urging that this 20 per cent duty be taken off this drugi I do not see how you can justify that. It is something for suffering humanity and you should let it in if it is at all possible.

If there is any way in which the government can facilitate a plentiful supply of equipment being made available in Canada to protect the lives and property of its citizens from fire, I think the government should take those steps.
