speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Since penicillin has been mentioned by the hon, member for Kootenay West, perhaps I should give a fairly full explanation of the situation because it is one which is naturally of very great concern to the people of Canada. Our present tariff item 206a(l) provides for duty free entry from all countries of serums, antitoxins, viruses, toxins, toxoids, vaccines and allergenic products, n.o.p., for parenteral administration in the diagnosis or treatment of diseases of man. There is a second section applying the same thing to animals.
Last June a United States company entered two importations of penicillin S-R, duty free, under tariff item 206a at the port of Windsor, Ontario. On July 15, 1949, the importer was advised by the Department of National Revenue that antibiotics including penicillin were not considered to be biological products, and were dutiable under tariff item 711, the item covering unenumerated goods, at the most-favoured-nation rate of 20 per cent. The importer appealed this ruling to the tariff board and the appeal was heard by the board on October 4, 1949. It is to be noted that tariff item 206a covered biological products. These products, however, were limited to those for parenteral administration-I looked up that word, and it means an injection under the skin-and to those manufactured under licence of the Department of Pensions and National Health, now the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The tariff board rendered its decision, which was actually in favour of penicillin being admitted duty free, with one dissenting opinion. The deputy minister of national revenue has now announced that he intends to apply to the Exchequer Court of Canada for leave to appeal from the decision of the tariff board on questions of law.
It was quite apparent, therefore, that the wording of tariff item 206a was too ambiguous to be continued in its present form, and it is now proposed to revise the wording to specify by name the products this item was originally intended to cover. As the minister stated in his budget speech, he is going to
Customs Tariff
refer the whole question of antibiotics to the tariff board for investigation and report under part I of the Tariff Board Act. It is felt that the present wording will meet this situation until the report of the board is tabled in parliament. Penicillin will therefore continue, as in the past, to be dutiable under tariff item 711 at the rate of 15 per cent under the British preferential tariff and 20 per cent under the most-favoured-nation tariff.
Now I want to go on to the next part. When penicillin was first developed, during the middle years of the war, the manufacture was started by the Americans to begin with, and we found we could not obtain penicillin from the United States sources. So as a matter of national security we encouraged the construction of laboratories in this country to undertake the manufacture of penicillin. These companies started operations in Canada in 1943; and when we speak of prices it is very interesting to see what happened to the price of penicillin and other antibiotics produced by these companies since that time. In 1943 they offered penicillin to the government at a price of $20 per 100,000 units. By 1944 the price had fallen to $7 per 100,000 units. Today the price to hospitals has been lowered to 19 cents per 100,000 units in 100,000-pnit vials, or 12 cents per 100,000 units in the million-unit vials. I think it is very definitely in the national interest that the manufacture of penicillin and other antibiotics, such as streptomycin, be continued in this country, and so some protection is deserved.
I have the figures here as to production. I will not name the companies, but of the three producing these antibiotics the value of the penicillin produced last year in one case was $768,000, in another $2 million and in the third $160,000. Two of the three companies produced other antibiotics, the value of production of one amounting to $2,323,000 and of the other to $64,000 making a total production worth $5,310,000 in this country, adequate to supply our own needs and actually leaving enough for export to the amount of $1,829,000.
In the past penicillin was classed under tariff item 708, not as one of these biological' products. This American company made a test case of it. All we are doing now, pending full investigation by the tariff board, is to continue in law what has been the practice. That is being done for two reasons, first because it has been the practice and second to protect this very important industry which-has grown up in Canada, which was developed at a time when we could not get penicillin from outside sources, and which

Customs Tariff
is adequate to meet our present needs. More than that, I believe the fact that the price has fallen from a high of $20 per 100,000 units in 1943 to a low of 12 cents to hospitals in 1950 is an indication that we have secured good results under this policy.

Can the minister say why penicillin is still under prescription, why it cannot be bought without a prescription? I have been asked this question many times. It comes in certain strengths, but apparently a prescription is still necessary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot give the answer as far as the medical end is concerned. One of the difficulties with penicillin, of course, is the fact that it deteriorates very quickly. One of the reasons this United States company was so anxious to dump penicillin in this country was this price war in the United States, and also a desire to get rid of a surplus of deteriorated penicillin. However, I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be a better person to ask why penicillin is still sold only by prescription.
Can the minister say what was the price of penicillin to hospitals in the beginning?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All the penicillin the hospitals got in 1943 came through the government, and the government bought it at $20. At that time penicillin was used only in military hospitals, because of short supply.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant if he is in a position to give us a brief analysis of the changes made in the tariff schedules? Those changes seem to be very few, and I wondered if there was a brief analysis available.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The only actual change in the entire schedule is the change in tinplate. That is the only instance in which there is a tariff increase.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then may I ask whether there are items in these schedules now before us in which there is no change .at all, or is there in some instances a change in the designations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There are many changes in numbers. I just gave an example. Item 206a included these biological products for injection into human beings, and a second section of the same item covered products for injection into animals. That now has been separated into two sections. Another example is potassium chlorate. There was a change in the tariff schedule in 1933, and the item read "all potassium chlorate imported into the country after July 1, 1933." That deadline is still carried in the tariff schedule,

though obviously it is of no significance seventeen years later; and that has been removed. The greater part of this job is cleaning up things like that, the exceptions being the gums and tinplate in the next section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words there has been some change in every item in the schedule, even if it is only the number of the items?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is quite right.
Regarding the tinplate item-[DOT]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the next section.

If I may enlighten the hon. member for York West, as one who has retailed penicillin for a goodly number of years, I may tell him that penicillin is available to the public in a strength up to 3,000 units for oral use; but its parenteral use is still under the direction of a doctor. As the hon. member will see, if it were available to the layman it could be used indiscriminately. I am sure that is the reason it is offered only to medical men for parenteral administration.

Thank you very much. I am sure the committee will be glad to have that information. Since penicillin is unlike the sulfa drugs, since it is not toxic or habitforming in any way, I wondered why a prescription was required, since apparently there is no possibility of an overdose.

speakerposition: stagedirection
Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is the resolution to which I should like to direct attention because of

the comments that have been made and editorials which have appeared in several new-papers in Canada, about tinplate. In this list covered by resolution 3, there are I think a total of 435 items. Almost all of them are changes in numbering or the removal of obsolete language or changes in designation to fit designations agreed upon at the Geneva trade conference. There are however two of them to which I should like to refer. The first is the duty on gum compound. This is item 254, which provides for duty-free entry under the British preferential and most-favourednation tariffs of various gums. Under the mostfavoured-nation tariff there is a 10 per cent duty applied if those duty-free gums are mixed before entry. That is one small change brought about by Geneva, that they now enter duty free. It is a small group, and not of much consequence.
The other group, tinplate, is a much more interesting example. Hon. members will recall that the object of negotiations during the 1947 discussions at Geneva was to reduce the general level of tariffs and eliminate tariff preferences on a mutually advantageous basis. Towards the end of these negotiations the United States requested the United Kingdom to give up the tariff preference it enjoyed in Canada on tinplate. The proposal did not originate with Canada. The United States requested it and it was the United Kingdom who agreed to this, and you will see the reason why not much objection was made. The United Kingdom agreed, and received in return tariff concessions from the United States in compensation for giving up this preference.
In order to facilitate the successful conclusion of United States, United Kingdom and Canadian trade negotiations, Canada agreed to the proposal that the British preferential tariff on tinplate be increased to 15 per cent, the same as the most-favoured-nation rate, thereby actually eliminating the preference. It was understood on all sides that when this change was made it would be of very little practical importance in trade between Canada and the United Kingdom. In the first place, the United Kingdom did not expect to be in a position, for many years in the post-war period, to export significant quantities of tinplate to Canada. In the second place, Canadian production had expanded to a point where we were supplying a very large part of our own requirements. Our present production of tinplate is in the neighbouhood of $35 million annually.
I shall give you the figures on imports. In 1947 our import of tinplate from all countries was valued at over $8 million, of which only
Customs Tariff
$107,000 worth came from the United Kingdom, and the remainder from the United States. Even since that time our production has steadily increased. During 1949, imports from all countries have dropped from $8 million in 1947 down to $3,800,000, all of which came from the United States except $68,000 from the United Kingdom. We produced this year between $35 million and $36 million of tinplate ourselves. Last year's import from the United Kingdom was only $68,000. You can see, therefore, that when the Americans requested the British to make this concession, the British realized it was a trivial concession. Every indication is that we shall have a still greater Canadian production, and that our small imports are going to dwindle still more.
If there is any interest in the figures, I can put on the record the monthly importation during 1949 of tinplate from Britain and the United States. Actually, it just shows the story I have given, a steady dwindling of imports from both countries down, as I said, to the $68,000 last year from the United Kingdom, when our own production amounted to $35 million.

Can the parliamentary
assistant say when we began to manufacture tinplate in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We manufactured it in a small way before the war, but it was during the war that the manufacture of tinplate began on a large scale. Since the war, when tin from Malaya became available, the Canadian steel companies went ahead with the manufacture of tinplate, using the latest electrolytic method.

The parliamentary assistant has been plausible, but I still do not think he has given a logical reason for this increase. I think he said the amount involved was inconsequential, so it does not matter. If the amount involved is only $68,000, why put the tariff on at all? The parliamentary assistant pointed out that the United States asked Great Britain to agree to this, and the British did so. The British have had the gun put to them quite a few times in the last few years. With ECA aid and things of that nature, how can they refuse some of these United States requests? I think half the people of Canada should realize that, despite the verbiage which the parliamentary assistant used to dress this up, it is a straight increase and a protectionist measure to protect the tinplate industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is very obvious, to anyone who gives the matter a little thought, that the British were horse-trading and did a good job of it. They secured these important

Customs Tariff
concessions in return tor the preference on tin which did not amount to anything. It is inconsequential so far as this country is concerned.
When one talks about ECA dollars, hon. members should realize that the leaders of the United States delegation have to satisfy the members of congress about the United States concessions, and here they could say that in return they secured the abolition of the British preference on tinplate. Our country did not ask for it. It was a matter arranged between the United Kingdom and the United States, and we gladly agreed because, as I say, it is inconsequential to this country owing to our greatly increased production of tinplate.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant if he knows anything about these wire and tape recording machines used for playbacks in checking speech in educational institutions? I want to know if a duty is charged against those things, and if so, why they are not on this free list No. 696. Needless to say I am not an expert on picking out the various items. What are the conditions that apply to these machines used for educational purposes? The minister was asked about this, and he said a considerable number of these machines were manufactured in Canada. I have made some inquiries, and I And there is only one machine manufactured in Canada. He said they were available from various sources, and I should like to know what those sources are. My information is that there is only one machine produced in Canada and that it is sold under different names. I am further informed that the price of a machine in the United States is about $125, Canadian funds, and that the price in Halifax is $270, a difference due to these various prohibitions. I should like to know whether the importer of such an item has to have an official permit before he can import it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: These dictating machines today come under item 414a. There has been no change in that item, but there is a 10 per cent duty on machines of British origin, and 20 per cent most-favoured-nation, with 25 per cent other nations. The United States, of course, is a most favoured nation. Pardon me, I am informed that the most-favourednation is 20 per cent, but the United States has another rate of 12 per cent. I believe last year the minister did say that these machines were made here. I understand that at least two firms make those machines in Canada.

Is this information correct that two firms are making them, or is only one firm making them and selling them under

different names? The minister mentioned several sources in Canada. What are they? What is the reason for the imposition of this tariff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have been trying to give all the information I can on the actual items that we have under review. It is information about these that I have here tonight. On an item such as the hon. member mentions I suggest that a question should be put on the order paper, and in that way he could obtain more information, because we could give the answer tomorrow or later.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant what in his opinion is the justification for having tariff charged on these things? Surely, if they are for educational purposes, for the use of schools and colleges, they should be treated in the same way as other things in 696.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano you could give us your opinion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have given my opinion quite often. The main reason we put on taxes is to raise revenue for the desirable services which hon. members ask for. For example, the hon. member for Saskatoon is asking for federal aid to education. Well, if we are going to give federal aid to education we shall have to find money somewhere, and it can only be found through taxation.
So far as the use of these dictaphones is concerned, the great bulk of their use is undoubtedly in business offices, and we tax most of the equipment used in business offices as a source of revenue, and this class of thing comes in that category.

I do not see what my views on education have to do with this kind of thing. So far as I am concerned, I confess a desire for federal aid to education, and I have no thought of changing my views. Does the reply of the parliamentary assistant mean that we are going to get federal aid to education? We already have a tariff placed against these machines, and I should like to know the justification for it. Must a Canadian school or university have an import licence before they can import these things at all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The answer to the second question is yes. The answer to the first question is that probably the hon. member did not understand my reply. That probably is the reason why hon. members, like the hon. member for Saskatoon, are continually making these demands for bigger expenditures, and have no realization at all that somehow, somewhere, the Minister of Finance has to find the money to finance these expenditures.

I used the example of education only because the hon. member has put forward on various occasions his thought that there should be financial aid from the federal government for education. That being the case, I would think that he should realize that somewhere, somehow, the federal government is going to have to find that revenue to maintain all these desirable projects.
I am informed that in Saskatchewan, for example, they very recently increased their sales tax from 2 per cent to 3 per cent for this very reason, not that they wanted to impose an extra tax on goods which may still be necessities, or used in schools or businesses, or in industry, but because they had to get extra revenue. Therefore again I say to him, as far as this matter of dictaphones is concerned, which is not an item covered by this resolution at all, that if he wants to secure more information on it he has only to ask the appropriate minister, the Minister of National Revenue. We have come here prepared to discuss every item on the schedule, but not to discuss policy or items which are not covered in these amendments.

Mr. Chairman, the avowed policy of this government, so far as I know, is not to charge tariff against these educational machines. I think my question was reasonable enough. Why is this item I have in mind not included among these other items for which the government itself has given us a precedent in the matter of allowing them in free? I am not asking for federal aid to education in this instance. I am asking the government to do away with something that is a drag upon education. Why should that one particular item regarding tape machines, or whatever the technical name is, not be on this list when there are on the free list many other things having to do with education? Personally I think it is a matter that has not been considered. I think it is carelessness on the part of the department concerned. I see no other reason. I believe it has not come to the attention of the government, or they have not given it consideration. If they had they would realize and see that it is simply one machine that should be free because of its similarity to the items that are free. I am not asking for anything; I am simply asking that the government follow its own precedent, the precedent of not charging tariff on educational machines. I do not see why we should have to pay $270 for a thing which, in the United States, is worth $125 in Canadian funds. I do not think that these remarks about the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan and what it is doing there are applicable or relevant to the matter under discussion. It is simply the same old story
Customs Tariff
of playing politics with a matter which in my opinion should be considered seriously. I am interested in the children of this country, and it has nothing whatsoever to do with politics, or with the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think the parliamentary assistant should give a little thought to the nature of the answer he has given to the hon. member for Saskatoon. The hon. member for Saskatoon asked why educational institutions have to pay this particular tax. His answer was that the government has to collect that tax from educational institutions so as to provide funds for federal aid for education, which it is not providing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is very good at playing on words. I do not think anybody in the committee except himself took that meaning out of my words.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is what the hon. member said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the hon. member is no more accurate than that in phrasing things he has just heard, I can understand why he is so loose in paraphrasing things that happened weeks or months ago.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
You said it; now you
straighten it out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Getting back to this question, it is quite true that the sales tax and excise tax are remitted on a great number of things used by educational institutions. To my knowledge there has never been a request from any educational institution of standing in the country for exemption for these dictaphones for recording and mechanical use by educational systems in Canada. If that request comes forward and is supported by a good case no doubt the minister will give careful consideration to it.
Just before we close this discussion, the assistant to the minister made the statement that these duties were imposed in order to raise revenue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is part of it.
I do not think that is all the reason. I think the reason is to protect our workmen against other goods coming in here and stopping them from manufacturing them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is a combination of these two.
Yes; it is to protect our men and secure their jobs for them.

Would the parliamentary assistant indicate to the committee briefly how much of the Geneva agreement has now been carried into effect, first by order in

Customs Tariff
council and second by statute, and what portion of the agreement may yet not be in effect in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am informed that of the almost 1,000 items on the Geneva schedule we have now implemented, through this and other changes, some 435, and we have carried out, more than perhaps any other country, most of the undertakings which we gave at Geneva; and that will be one of the points which we will raise at Torquay, the fact that we have taken the lead. That is why we are anxious to get this through. We have taken the lead in trying to implement in our tariff schedules the concessions agreed to at Geneva. The fact is that out of almost 1,000 items we have implemented 435.
That is to say, there are roughly 565 that have not been carried into effect. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, on which further negotiations will take place at Torquay.
As to the 435, assuming the enactment of a bill to give effect to the resolutions now before the house, how many of the 435 will then rest on a statutory basis, how many on an order in council basis?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The entire 435 will then rest on a statutory basis, and as the other undertakings are agreed to at Torquay they too will be put on a statutory basis.

On a former item the parliamentary assistant said, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Moose Mountain, that he would explain on this item how the tariff and dumping duties benefited western farmers. I should like to hear his explanation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It was not on this item. However, I might be permitted to revert to resolution 2. The hon. member for Moose Mountain asked if there was any instance where these dumping duties helped Canadian farmers.
An hon Member: Western farmers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, western farmers. This matter connected with fruits and vegetables certainly is one which concerns the western farmers whom I know in my province. At Geneva the question of the protection of a country's fruit and vegetable farming industry during periods when it is in production was thoroughly discussed. Section 14 of the present Customs Tariff is being repealed and the new section 14 is being substituted therefor.
The new section authorizes the minister of National Revenue to fix the period when imported fresh fruits and vegetables are to be subject to the specific rates of duty pro-

vided for in the various tariff items covering fresh fruits and vegetables. The minister is also authorized to do something he could not do before, namely to apply it regionally. This is important in Canada where the various crops come in at different periods of the year. During those periods which are designated in the Geneva agreement by time, the length of the period in which these extra duties can be applied, the minister can regionally or nationally, by means of this extra specific duty, protect the Canadian farmer growing these fruits and vegetables.
Up until we concluded this Geneva agreement we had an agreement with the United States which, of course, this agreement now supersedes. That agreement called for three split periods for cabbage, carrots and beets. We were asked for the split period because of the nature of our problem. First in the season is when our own hothouses are producing these fruits and vegetables for the Canadian market, during which time they have to have a measure of protection against surplus coming in from the United States. Then there is the period later in the year, when there is field production, when we have to have similar protection.
That has now been extended. We now have a split period for beans, cabbage, carrots, beets, cauliflower, celery and lettuce.

Returning to the matter I mentioned a moment ago, I should like to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to something he said. His statement was that, so far as he was aware, no application had been made by any educational institution. I am prepared to accept his word in regard to his lack of awareness, but not as to the other matter-because an application was made.
I shall place on record, to just such an application by a professor at Dalhousie university, the reply from some assistant, apparently, of the Minister of National Revenue. This reply is dated at Ottawa, March 20, 1950, and states:
I wish to inform you that the "Revere" magnetic tape recorder, per descriptive illustration submitted, manufactured by Revere Camera Company, Chicago, Illinois, a general purpose recorder for use in the recording of sound on a magnetized tape, incorporating provision for play-back thereof, is considered to be an article of a class or kind made in Canada, and, therefore, not admissible under tariff item 696 under any circumstance, but rated for duty under tariff item 445k, at 22J per cent ad valorem, most-favoured-nation tariff, subject, in addition, to the consumption, or sales tax of 8 per cent levied on the duty-paid value . . . The above magnetic tape recorder is restricted importation under the provisions of the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act and may only be imported under permit from the emergency import control division, Department of Finance, 490 Sussex street, Ottawa.

And then Mr. Abbott wrote, in reply, I believe, to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on some date in 1950-1 have not the exact date:
With regard to the duties and taxes, I am informed by the Department of National Revenue that these wire and tape recorders would not be classified under tariff Item 696, which allows educational equipment to be imported into Canada duty free-
And I would ask the parliamentary assistant to listen to the reason given.
-because these machines are manufactured in Canada and are available from several sources.
The point I made, and which the parliamentary assistant has not cleared up, is that it is suggested that these machines do not come from several sources in Canada, but rather that one machine is made and sold under various names, giving colour to the suggestion that they come from various sources. I am not sure whether that is correct or not, but I presume it is the business of someone in the department to find out. I would ask for that information. If it is true then in all reason, leaving out all those wisecracks about politics, the C.C.F., and everything else, in the interests of educational organizations in this country I see no reason why that one particular item should be picked to be omitted from the list of items to be allowed in free under the heading of items used for educational purposes.

Mr. Chairman, before we pass this item, there is one comment I should like to make. Men can keep on repeating fallacies until they begin to believe they are true. One of the fallacies constantly repeated by ministers in the House of Commons is that all payments must come from taxation.
Just to give the parliamentary assistant something to think about, may I read from the proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce in 1939, the official publication thereof. At page 54 I find this:
That is the theory that governmental expenditure must be made through the medium of taxation.

Governmental expenditure may be
made either through the medium of taxation or through borrowing, or through the issue of currency . . .
I hope we do not hear any more of this parrot repetition of the fallacy that everything must be paid for out of taxation.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Research Council Act to provide for the appointment of an additional vice-president of the national research council, and to bring the act into conformity with the Patent Act as to the definition of "invention."

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL VICE-PRESIDENT   DEFINITION OF "INVENTION"
speechtext: Is the parliamentary assistant making a statement?

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllraiih (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL VICE-PRESIDENT   DEFINITION OF "INVENTION"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation of which this resolution forms the basis is not extensive in scope. Hon. members will recall that the Research Council Act was passed in 1924 and amended in 1946. By the 1946 amendment provision was made for the appointment of two vicepresidents, one vice-president, scientific, and one vice-president, administration. In 1947 when the operation of the atomic energy project at Chalk River was placed under the jurisdiction of the research council the man in charge of that project was given the position of vice-president, scientific.
The result is that as far as the research council itself is concerned the one position of vice-president, administration, is filled but there is no position to which a person could be appointed to have similar jurisdiction over
2190	HOUSE OF
Research Council Act
the scientific end of the operation. It is desired that there should be a vice-president having charge of the scientific work of the research council other than that of the atomic energy project, and the legislation proposes to create this additional position of vicepresident, scientific.
The second part of the resolution simply deals with the definition of the term "invention." It will be recalled that the Research Council Act was enacted in 1924, whereas our patent legislation is more recent. The definition of "invention" in the Patent Act is wider and gives more complete protection than the definition in the Research Council Act. It is proposed by this legislation to bring the two definitions into line so that the research council definition will follow that of the Patent Act.
This is particularly important when one remembers that under the legislation patents of invention by technical officials of the research council vest in the council. With the current developments in chemistry and atomic energy it is particularly important that the definition be wide enough to include compositions of matter as well as apparatus and other mechanical inventions. The present definition is somewhat weak in this respect.
There is one other slight change being made by the proposed legislation which has to do with the term "national research council." The present legislation does not provide for the use of that term although it has been in general use since 1925 when it was authorized by an order in council. It is proposed to give its use legislative authority. I do not think there is any more I can usefully say on the resolution stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this
resolution was discussed about two weeks ago I was not present, but I have read the statements made at that time and I must say that I heartily agree with much of the criticism and also with much of the praise offered on that occasion. This question of extending the war veterans allowance to other than Canadians is not a new matter to come before this house. I am very pleased indeed that this benefit is being extended to these men, most of whom are imperials, who have now become citizens of our country. This is something for which the veterans committee has fought on many occasions. If you were to go through the records of that committee for the past fifteen years I think you would find there was not a session during which the granting of the war veterans allowance to imperials was not brought to the attention of that committee and the government. I think it is only a matter of justice that these men should be included.
I have sometimes wondered just what was the reason for this change of heart, why after all these years it should be recognized now that these men are entitled to consideration. I have a feeling that it may have been brought about as a result of the matter being dealt with at the time Newfoundland was brought into confederation. I know one demand made by Newfoundland at that time was that the imperials in that province be granted the war veterans allowance. It would have been an anomalous situation in the rest of Canada if the imperials in Newfoundland were granted the benefits of the war veterans allowance and those in the rest of Canada did not receive the same treatment. I wonder whether it was on that account, and perhaps the minister will tell us, that after all these years these men have received the benefits to which they are entitled.
Now that this act is being amended, Mr. Chairman, I think the government and the department could very well have made some other amendments. I believe they were forced to make the amendment regarding imperials, as I say, owing to the fact that the allowance was granted in Newfoundland. When these amendments were being made, why was it that, after all these years, and after the pressure which has been brought to bear through the different veterans committees, the Canadians who were in England during the first war were not included? They had just as much reason, and perhaps more, to be included as the imperials. It is not necessary for me to argue this point. A reading of the record of debates in this house, as well as the record of debates in the veterans
War Veterans Allowance Act committees, will reveal the reasons why Canadians in England during the first war should be included. Many of our men who went overseas with the first contingent in the first war suffered a great deal on Salisbury plains. It has been recorded that more men died of disease and exposure on Salisbury plains during the first winter than were killed by bombs in England during the first war.
There are men who never even got to England-and I am not opposing this because I was strongly in favour of dual pensions-in the first war and the second war, who are receiving war veterans allowance. It does seem to me that the men who served in England are as deserving as the men who were not allowed to go to France, for many good reasons, and they have just as much right to receive the war veterans allowance as those men who served in Canada only. It was brought out in our committee that there are men, whose only service apart from training was in France after the armistice was signed, men who served in labour battalions, men who were on the war graves commission, and men who were sent to fill up battalions before they went into Germany, who are entitled to war veterans allowances. Yet the men who served four and five years in England during the first war, and who suffered on Salisbury plains, are denied the war veterans allowance. I do think that the minister, if he had wished to do a complete job, could easily have included in these amendments the Canadians who served in England.
Arguments have been advanced for increases in the basic rates, but I am not going to take up the time of the house by repeating those. They are all recorded in Hansard. Then there was a point brought up the other evening, I think by the member for Nanaimo, in connection with the widows of imperials who died before they had put in the twenty years' residence required in this country. I have often wondered just why the twenty-year period was chosen. We have been told, that the War Veterans Allowance Act is a form of old age pension act. We know that in the Old Age Pensions Act a man had to be in Canada twenty years before he qualified for the old age pension. Just why we should say a soldier should have to be in Canada twenty years, I do not know. The War Veterans Allowance Act is not an old age pension act. When it was first granted, it may have had some resemblance to an old age pension act, but it has been changed so radically that today it cannot be considered as a half-sister or half-brother of the Old Age Pensions Act. I believe the minister should consider reducing that period of twenty years,
2194	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act and allowing those widows whose husbands were here the shorter period of time to have the benefit of the war veterans allowance.
Under the old age pension act in the United States, if a person is a resident in some of the states five years, he receives the benefit of the old age pension. In some other states one need only be a resident for one year to receive the pension benefit. Under our citizenship act anyone who comes to Canada can become a Canadian citizen in five years, so I think the five-year residence period could easily have been adopted under the War Veterans' Allowance Act for these imperials. After all an imperial soldier would be a British subject, and the five-year period would suffice to qualify. The widow of an imperial veteran who died after five years' residence in Canada could very well have been granted the war veterans' allowance. It would not have involved a large amount of money, because I think the minister will agree with me that there is not a large number of these widows, and as time goes on no doubt there will be fewer.
So far as the second part of the bill is concerned, I quite agree with the minister that the act could be better administered if it were put on a district basis. The district war veterans allowance authorities are given practically the same authority as Ottawa has. They can award, increase, decrease, annul or suspend an allowance, according to the act. All this is subject to review in Ottawa. I hope that there will be a careful supervision by the department in Ottawa to make sure that all parts of the country are being treated alike. We know that in certain provinces these matters are not always dealt with in the same way. I warn the minister he will have to be careful to see that the administration across Canada is uniform, and that there is no discrimination so far as any part is concerned.
There is another matter which I believe the minister might have taken into consideration, and that is in connection with the veterans who are indigent and live in the United States. If they come to Canada, they are required to have three months' residence here-

Mr. Chairman, I was particularly glad to hear the hon. member for Royal speak tonight, because it has often appeared to me that hon. members from British Columbia particularly were the most difficult people that the government had to deal with in this house. I do not know whether we have a higher standard of living in British Columbia, or whether it is that we are hard to get along with and expect more. However, it is pleasant to know that in these representations to the government the members from British Columbia have the support of at least some of the other provinces in the dominion.
Out in British Columbia we feel that there is some merit in the contention of the veterans' organizations out there that our war veterans allowance does not come up to the payment that we make to old age pensioners. I am quite sure that the minister himself is greatly concerned on that point, because nobody likes to have it implied that we treat our war veterans in a more niggardly way than we treat our old age pensioners. We realize that the veterans get paid at an earlier age, and there are other advantages that are not given to the old age pensioners. I might say that our old age pensioners in British Columbia get hospitalization care, which is something we in British Columbia are proud of.
The minister might consider the value of establishing a standing committee on veterans affairs, as has been suggested so many times in the house. We can realize that when he

goes to cabinet he finds that there are 15 or 20 other ministers there who think that they need money just as badly as he does. It must be quite a competition and no doubt the minister who can make the most strenuous representation as to need is the one who gets the most consideration. I was wondering whether the minister would consider the virtue of having a veterans' committee standing behind him to support him in his very able endeavours to obtain more funds for his old comrades whom, I am sure, he has taken care of in a magnificent way since he became minister.
There is one thing that I should like to say to the minister in regard to the payment of war veterans allowances to imperial veterans. This is a matter that the Canadian Legion has been pressing for a great many years. It is greatly to the minister's credit that he has finally been able to submit arguments to his colleagues and has been able to prevail upon their better judgment, and thus has been successful in obtaining that concession. It does seem to me that, so far as the widows are concerned, if the man did not live the twenty years in Canada he really must have aged more quickly because of his service in France than the others, because he was not able to stand up for twenty years afterwards. I do not think there would be too much money inyolved. I think the minister would probably agree with that. I do not think there would be any principle involved that would not be compatible with his views and with the views of the government. As there is not too much money involved I would ask him to see if he could not persuade his colleagues to meet the wishes of the Canadian Legion in this regard.
I think Canadians are particularly proud of the veterans legislation we have. It seems that every time we pass legislation some members of the opposition rise in their places and say it is too little and too late. I do not want to be placed in that position because, in my opinion, this government and the minister have done a tremendous job for the veterans. Within the confines of the money that we are able to secure from the Canadian people in the form of taxes, the Department of Veterans Affairs have done a magnificent job in administering it. So long as I have been in the house there has been nothing but first-class administration of this department. I am particularly proud to have had a small part-and probably a very small part in supporting the government since I came here in 1945-in this legislation; but I would ask the minister to give these matters
War Veterans Allowance Act all the favourable consideration he possibly can. This is a debt which the people of Canada owe and will gladly pay.

Mr Chairman, as one of those who spoke when this matter was up before on April 20 I intend to take only a few minutes, and to confine my remarks to just one subject. I fully realize that on the evening of April 20 the minister set it out clearly and seemed to take a very firm position. But I think he will realize also that there was a feeling ,in the house that somehow or other the position he took was not right. Several examples were given. For example, I gave two instances of imperial veterans who came to this country both in 1925, bringing their wives with them. The first veteran died in 1944, having lived here 19 years. His widow is now in need, but she will not qualify. The other veteran managed to live until 1946. His widow will qualify. Why not treat the two widows alike? In both instances you have a widow who probably herself came from the United Kingdom and has become a Canadian citizen like the rest of us. In both cases you may have widows whose sons served in the second war. It did seem to all of us, I am sure, the other evening, that this point of discrimination was not fair.
I say, Mr. Chairman, the reason I took to my feet to say the same thing that two previous speakers have said is that I did think it desirable to reconstruct that atmosphere that was here before, in the hope that the minister has thought about the situation in the meantime. I do not wish to labour this matter. However, I have listened with a good deal of attention to what other hon. members have said. There are just two thoughts I would leave with the minister, and concerning which he may have something to say later on. I believe the worst kind of discrimination lies in the fact that the widow of the veteran of the first war who saw service in England, even under the present arrangement, is not entitled to the war veterans allowance. I suggest that even yet the minister should consider preparing a regulation which would wipe out that kind of discrimination.
Then, I am also concerned-and I use that word advisedly-about decentralization of administration. I have known the minister for a long time, and I have never had any difficulty in arriving at a fair arrangement under the legislation. I have found in many cases however that when one gets down to the provincial level, where the act is administered, there is difficulty. I should like to have my mind clarified as to whether decentralization means that the minister wants to divorce himself from certain responsibilities and if, on the other hand, this change would


pave the way for more jobs, more patronage and a more inefficient administration at the provincial level.
It is my view that the minister should retain as much power as possible to direct and supervise this legislation. I do not believe decentralization will make for better administration; I believe it will mean greater inefficiency. It will divorce the minister and the board in Ottawa from many decisions which will be made provincially, and in my opinion this move will not react in the best interest of the veteran.
I have agreed with the minister on many occasions. We have agreed to have certain things done, but when these matters have reached the provincial level it appeared that officials at that level had more authority than the minister had, or than the department in Ottawa had. The result has been a good deal of confusion-and I am not referring to veterans allowances, but to other problems.
I would ask the minister to clarify my mind as to the meaning of decentralization of administration as it is applied here. I should like to see the minister responsible to the House of Commons, where the basic legislation is written, placed in a position where he can come to the house and accept responsibility for any decision made by his department at any time and at any level.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do suggest the minister should answer the various suggestions that have been placed before him. When the resolution was under consideration two weeks ago tonight I raised several points, and I have no intention of repeating them now. Toward the end of the sitting, however, several of us did suggest that further consideration be given to the eligibility of the widow of the imperial veteran.
Thinking the matter over during these two weeks I am convinced we were right when we said everyone thought the test would be whether the veteran came here twenty years ago. If he came here in 1930 or before, then he should be considered as qualified. As a matter of fact I do not know why we should insist upon his having been here for twenty years. But if that time is set, then surely the test for the widow should be whether the husband came here in 1930 or before. If he did, she should be considered eligible. Otherwise there are many of these widows who cannot qualify for the allowance. In my judgment that would be a most unfair situation.
I believe it is the wish of the house and certainly of all veteran members in the house that the legislation should be made to include the widow of any imperial veteran who came

here at least twenty years ago, as was suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
Then, I hope the minister will explain whether or not these payments are to be retroactive. I suggested two weeks ago that they be dated back to December 10, when the parliamentary assistant made the announcement. I would point out that for many months now investigations have been under way in the department. All imperials who were thought to be eligible have been asked to fill out forms and to give information. I would hope the allowance would be made retroactive at least to the date of the announcement last December.
I should like to have some clarification on the proposal to decentralize the administration. It has been explained that this means that decisions will be made out in the districts as to whether or not veterans or widows are eligible for allowances. Personally, I believe this is a wise change. But what is to be the position once a veteran is granted that allowance in the district? Will it then be possible for the war veterans allowance board in Ottawa to upset that decision, if it is favourable to the veteran?
I submit that if the veteran can qualify before the district officer or the district board, or whatever body is set up, then he should get the allowance without being placed in danger of having it upset by a board of review here in Ottawa. It is all right to have a board of review in Ottawa to look into the cases where veterans have lost out; but I hope we will not have a condition whereby many of these veterans will receive their allowances in the local districts and then be faced with the possibility of having them taken away by the board of review in Ottawa who have not seen the veteran and who could not possibly have the same understanding of the conditions he faces. The minister has not made clear what the position will be with regard to this review board and I hope he will do so this evening.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before this resolution is carried I should like to say a word or two. I have received many requests from veterans' organizations in my constituency and I wish to add my voice to those that have been raised already and urge the minister to include the widows of imperial veterans in this amendment. I am not going to enlarge on the subject because matters affecting veterans are always well taken care of by the veteran members in this house and it is not necessary for one who is not a veteran of either war, like myself, to deal with matters with which perhaps I may not be as familiar
War Veterans Allowance Act as with other matters. But I do urge the minister to give favourable consideration to this request. I do not believe the cost would be great, and even if it were he would simply be doing justice to those widows whose husbands passed away before the government extended these war veterans' allowances to imperial veterans.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer again to a case I have mentioned on many occasions, particularly during the last session. I had considerable correspondence with the minister and with the war veterans' allowance board in connection with this case. This was a case where the income was not revealed and it was necessary ultimately to take the case to court and prosecute the war veteran concerned. I am glad that the case has been settled and I want to tell the minister that I appreciate very much what in my opinion has been a generous settlement. It was the wife of the veteran rather than the veteran himself who corresponded with me. She told me that the lawyer prosecuting was on her side as well as on the other side. Again I wish to thank the minister for the satisfactory settlement that has been made of what I believe was a somewhat difficult case.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
I should like to say one further word if I may. I heartily approve of the grant of the $500,000 that was provided last year to supplement payments under the War Veterans Allowance Act, but I should like to reiterate the objections I have taken to the administration of that act. The parliamentary assistant has done his best to correct many of the mistakes that have been made, but it is my belief that a more simplified form of administration should be brought into effect.
I have seen the forms and I have listened to the investigators questioning war veterans allowance applicants or recipients. I know of one case in my riding of a man eighty-four years of age. I will not say that the advice he received from me was particularly good, but with that advice he had the advice of the Canadian Legion and two lawyers to enable him to fill out the form correctly. If my memory serves me aright he was granted a supplementary allowance of $10 per month until the end of September.
I am urging that the payment of these allowances be made more readily available. It should not be necessary for a veteran eighty-four years of age to have to go through all this red tape in order to secure the allowance until the end of September. At that time he will have to apply again and go to the Canadian Legion or to other people in order to have it extended for another short

War Veterans Allowance Act period. I think it is the wish of this parliament and of the people of Canada that this supplementary allowance should be paid during the remaining lifetime of a man eighty-four years of age in order to bring him up to the maximum of the amount received by an old age pensioner in my province.
The regulations should be more reasonable. This particular veteran served in three wars. I do not believe in calling this a burnt out pension; I believe it is something to which these men are entitled as of right and the amount they receive should at least be equal to that given our older citizens who receive it without having to go through all this red tape.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe there are nineteen returned soldier organizations and auxiliaries in my constituency and I do not think it is necessary for me to say how many requests I have received in connection with the payment of these allowances to widows of imperial veterans. I cannot help but support what has been said already in regard to this matter. I realize there are some complications and it may be difficult to find the proper solution. After listening to the discussion of a week ago I have reached the firm belief that a veterans committee should be set up so that we may go more thoroughly into this question and have more information than we are able to get in the house itself.
The Department of Veterans Affairs has done a wonderful job and the minister is to be congratulated. I have no complaints to make because I have been welcomed by all officials in the department. I feel that everything possible should be done to carry out what is an obligation to a certain extent to the widows of imperial veterans or of other allied forces who fought with us in the first war. Take a widow fifty-five years old. If she has been working at all she may be able to draw unemployment insurance, and that department will have to pay. If she cannot secure help from that particular department there is the widow's pension for which she may be able to qualify. If she can, naturally another department will have to pay. Then there are the social services of the municipalities towards which both the dominion and provincial governments contribute. She may be able to qualify for help there. In one way or another she will have to receive help from some government source. I think it is only right and proper that we should take this matter under consideration and do everything possible for the widows of imperial veterans and their allied associates.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
As an imperial veteran who has had a good deal to do with imperial veterans
[Mr. Crulckshank.l

in Canada for a number of years I should like to endorse what has been said by the last two speakers, particularly the member for Fraser Valley, as to the plight of widows of imperial veterans. I do not know how many are in distress but I assure you that several of them need assistance. I think it is rather degrading that the widows of men who served so nobly in the 1914-18 war must resort to charity or to the support of city councils in our smaller towns in order to live. As long as that blot remains it is most difficult for those who served in both wars to feel honestly and sincerely happy that everything possible is being done for these people. Our comrades who married these women have now passed on. I feel it is up to us who remain to fight for their widows. I am proud and pleased that the Canadian Legion women's auxiliaries right across the dominion have taken up the cudgels on their behalf. I appeal to the minister before it is too late to incorporate some protection in the bill for these widows that will place them at least on an equal basis with the widows of Canadian veterans since the service of their husbands burnt them out before their time.
As to the $10 bonus that has been given, in common with all other veterans I have noticed the small number who actually receive it. I feel that the red tape attached to the giving of the bonus should be lessened somewhat and that there should not be quite so strict an investigation into the needs of the person applying. I feel that many of these veterans are denied the extra $10 merely because they own a little home or get the odd job as a janitor and so on to help them struggle along. I did not think it was ever the intention of the house or the minister to make it so difficult to secure the extra bonus. I ask the minister to consider lessening the strings attached to the giving of the $10 in this measure, and also to look after the widows of imperial veterans.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had the privilege a week ago of attending a conference of imperial veterans from my riding and many adjoining ridings of western Ontario. I want to assure the minister that there was considerable jubilation over the prospect of this legislation being made effective and the possibility of the imperial veterans receiving the veterans allowance. They felt it was a victory and they thought 'much of the credit for it went to the work which veterans organizations had been carrying on for fifteen years. My information from them was that they had been fighting for at least fifteen years to secure this legislation. They were concerned about the plight of widows, but I think the position they took was a rather

unfortunate reflection on the way in which veterans have been getting assistance. They took the position that under the present circumstances it would be unwise for them to press for any further advantages than were provided in the proposed legislation. They were afraid to press the claims of the widows lest in doing so they should delay the passage of the legislation.
Their one concern was that the imperial veterans should first secure legislation in their favour, and that once it was placed on the statute books they would then push for improvements. The feature of it which struck me as rather unfortunate was the impression that the only way in which veterans can secure such legislation is by continually pushing the government until finally it surrenders to their claims. Their feeling was that they would get this and then they would start pressing the government in order to get something for the widows. As an outsider my suggestion is that from the standpoint of the government it would be much more to their credit to make some of these concessions without veterans having to push the government for a number of years in order to secure what they want.
They raised two questions which I should like the minister to answer. I think I know the answers, which I was able to give to them, but it would be satisfying to have the minister put them on record. There appeared to be some doubt whether imperial veterans who qualify for this benefit in every respect except that they are not sixty years of age, who are incapacitated, in hospital, indigent, without any means of support, would be eligible for veterans allowance under the act in the same way as other veterans. The second question they raised was just what procedure imperial veterans should take in order to be sure of getting the benefits as soon as possible. What procedure are they expected to follow in order to be eligible to receive the benefits at the earliest possible date? Those are the two questions that were raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
First of all I should like to acknowledge the suggestions that have been made in the twenty-five speeches made two weeks ago and tonight. A good deal of the discussion has been partly directed at the resolution and partly at the War Veterans Allowance Act. I make no complaint whatsoever about that. I mention it merely as a preface to this suggestion. If the committee is willing, I should like to see the resolution moved forward tonight. I do not think the committee would expect me to deal in full with the many questions
War Veterans Allowance Act raised concerning the act. I shall take a moment to mention a number of the special points made about the resolution. If I miss any that were made two weeks ago or this evening I can assure hon. members that I shall be glad to deal with them at a later stage.
The other evening the hon. member for Nanaimo asked if I could state the number of widows who have resided in Canada for twenty years but whose husbands died before they had acquired that length of residence. I regret to say it is not possible to make anything like an accurate estimate of that number. The survey made by our department and the organizations that have been named dealt primarily with veterans. As hon. members know, in all our veterans legislation any benefits accruing to wives or widows come to them through their veteran-husbands, when alive, or after their death. In that connection, therefore, I reiterate what I said two weeks ago. In this resolution and the bill which will follow it we are placing every British and allied veteran who has been resident in Canada for twenty years on exactly the same footing, for all purposes with respect to war veterans allowance, as the Canadian-born or those domiciled in Canada before they enlisted. If we do that for the veterans then I repeat that we would be creating some inequity if we made some special arrangements on behalf of widows for whom we have no such arrangements under any other of our veterans legislation. I might add, further to what I said in reply to this question, that the understanding of the organizations which have worked with us for at least the last two years in studying this problem, that is the imperial division of the Canadian Legion and the British-Canadian Veterans Association of the Veterans' Council of Canada- headed by that very capable gentleman to whom the hon. member for Wentworth paid tribute the other evening-has been exactly on that basis. That is verified by some suggestions put out by their respective periodicals in advance of this legislation coming into effect.
Then in reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South I would say that as the act now stands the minister has no authority whatever to influence the award of any war veterans allowance in any degree. I should like to reassure him, and others who mentioned the matter, that there will be uniformity in the administration of the act under the plan suggested. The decision will be reached in the district, but it will be a joint decision where in difficult cases it is necessary for the district authority to consult with one or more members of the
2200	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways-Auditors board. There will be no division of authority as between the board in Ottawa and the district authority as far as assessing a claim is concerned.
Then the suggestion was made that the allowance should be retroactive. It was announced that when the act goes into operation it was the intention to have payments begin as of the first of this fiscal year. As has been suggested here, a great many of these applications have come into our district offices, either through calls or in letters, since the parliamentary assistant made the announcement at the end of last session. Perhaps most of them have come in by now. When this legislation receives the royal assent and the districts can then complete the work already started, it is our intention that those who have applied, whether formally or informally, prior to or by April 1, 1950, and whose applications shall be approved, will receive the allowance as from April 1.
I think 1 shall leave the other matters until a later stage, and again I assure hon. members that at that time I shall be glad to discuss them fully.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: Would the minister explain a little more clearly what he means by a joint decision? Does that mean that an applicant in Vancouver must go before some board in the Vancouver district, but that such board will not have power to grant the allowance; that he will have to wait for approval by somebody here in Ottawa? If that is the case not very much time will be gained by having these decisions made in the districts. My understanding was that the board in the district would have power to make a decision, one purpose being that in this way payment would be made more quickly. Now, apparently, someone here in Ottawa is to be involved in that decision; someone here will have a part in it. subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN

tMr. Gregg.]

evening. In those cases the local authority will consult without delay with the visiting member or members of the board in order to reach a decision, and when that decision is reached it will be put into effect.

speechtext: We shall go into committee of supply and take up the estimates of transport. If we conclude that we shall go ahead with the estimates of veterans affairs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Friday, May 5, 1950
